t: a man would meet a woman in the market, etc. Even if he met a woman in a public place, by chance, they could marry at once by their consent, without any formal act preceding it.
and has relations with her privately. Without witnesses, who give the relations formal effect (below halakhah 2).
once the Torah was given, Israel were commanded, etc. The Torah commanded that the act of betrothal, performed before witnesses, precede the marriage.

before the giving of the Torah. The institution of marriage existed even before the Torah's command on the matter. This law has significance even after the giving of the Torah, for the rules of marriage among gentiles ("Noahides"); see Hilchot Melakhim 9:7-8.
and these acquisitions. The act of acquisition, which the Scripture expresses with the words "when he takes."
by money, or by document, or by relations. All the ways of acquisition are explained below in chapter 3.

and all three are Torah law. The acquisition by each of them takes effect by Torah law. The wording here follows the final edition as corrected by Rambam (Responsa Birkat Avraham 44); at first he wrote: "by relations and by document by Torah law, and by money by rabbinic law." See below 3:20 and the explanation there.
liable to the death penalty of the court. For the details of the punishment see Hilchot Issurei Biah 1:6.
a kedeshah. A prostitute.

anyone who has relations with a woman for the sake of harlotry, without betrothal, receives lashes. For every act of relations without betrothal is a harlot's act and is forbidden (Maggid Mishneh). Some explained that it speaks only of a woman who is available to harlotry with the public (Yad Peshutah, based on Hilchot Naarah Betulah 2:17, Hilchot Issurei Biah 18:2).
everything whose relations the Torah forbade and for whose relations it imposed karet. The death penalty at the hands of Heaven.

and they are the ones mentioned in the portion Acharei Mot. In which the severe forbidden relations are detailed (for their details see Hilchot Issurei Biah 1:4-7, and see the listing of commandments at the head of that unit of halakhot); some of them also carry the death penalty of the court.

that are forbidden by tradition and whose prohibition is rabbinic. Their prohibition was handed down in the tradition of halakhah and is not explicit in the Torah, and therefore the level of prohibition is that of a rabbinic enactment.
secondary relations. Forbidden relations of the second degree (for their punishment and force see Hilchot Issurei Biah 1:8).
and this one has no cutoff. There is no stopping point to her prohibition, for even the generations above her are forbidden as secondary relations.
only. And not the generations above her.
prohibitions of negative commandments. Those whose relations the Torah forbade with the word "not," without the punishment of karet.
a zonah. A woman who had relations with a man she is forbidden to marry or with a challal, or who is not Jewish (Hilchot Issurei Biah 18:1).
a challalah. One born of relations forbidden to the priesthood, or who was forbidden to priests and had relations with a priest (ibid. 19:1).
to a mamzer. One born of forbidden incestuous relations (ibid. 15:1).
and an Israelite woman to an Ammonite and Moabite. For converts from those nations are forbidden to marry Israelite women (for more see ibid. 12:17-18).
one whose testicles are crushed or whose organ is cut off. Whose testicles were crushed or whose male organ was severed (ibid. 16:3).
and his divorcee after she married another. That her first husband is forbidden to take her back (see Hilchot Gerushin 11:12).

and a yevamah who married a stranger while the yavam's claim on her still stands. A woman whose husband died without offspring and who is obligated by the Torah to marry one of his brothers; as long as the brother has not performed chalitzah for her, she is forbidden to everyone (for her prohibition to a stranger see Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 2:18).

a chalutzah is like a divorcee, etc. A yevamah for whom the yavam performed chalitzah is permitted thereby to marry another. But the Sages forbade her to marry a priest, because she resembles a divorcee (for her prohibition see Hilchot Issurei Biah 17:7).
and the Nethinim. The Gibeonites, who were from the nations of Canaan and converted by deceit, and were given to the service of the Temple.
they are like mamzerim. For the Sages decreed on them the prohibition of entering the congregation, like mamzerim.
and in Hilchot Issurei Biah. 12:22-24.

an Egyptian and an Edomite. Even if they converted, they are forbidden to marry Israelites until the third generation after their conversion (for their prohibition see Hilchot Issurei Biah 12:19). And a woman who has had relations, to a high priest. For her prohibition see ibid. 17:13.

and a negative commandment derived from a positive one. These prohibitions were learned from the general form of a positive commandment, and therefore are not counted as negative prohibitions but as positive commandments.
they are only like a wart. As if they grew because of a wart, which tends to grow hair regardless of maturity.
in the places known for growing hair. The pubic area (for a detailed definition see below halakhot 16-17). Second: In our time. From the age of twelve years and upward.
she is called a na'arah for six full months. She is called a na'arah only during this period of six months.
the day of completion. The day of fulfillment, the last day.
and between na'arut and majority there are only six months. For majority is not defined by particular signs, but by the time that has passed since she became a na'arah.
an aylonit. A woman whose sexual development is defective (for the signs of an aylonit see below halakhah 6).
she is an aylonit. And she is treated as an adult (see below halakhah 5).
thirty-five years. Which is the majority of a person's years, out of a lifespan of seventy years (see Psalms 90:10, Niddah 47b).
who has no breasts. Whose breasts did not develop.
and has difficulty during intercourse. Intercourse is hard and painful for her.
the lower abdomen. A protruding area at the edge of the abdomen.
she is called an adult. For the matter of punishments for transgressions of the Torah, and likewise for the matter of mi'un (refusal; see Hilchot Gerushin 11:4).
when she brings her hand behind her. When she stretches her hand backward.
and a fold is formed at the place of the breast. The breast will protrude (Commentary on the Mishnah, Niddah 5:8).
and when the head of the breast turns dark. When the areas around the nipples become dark (ibid.).
the tip of the breast. The edge of the breast, the nipple (ibid.).
the head of the nose of the breast. The protrusion at the end of the nipple.
like a ball. A circle (see Tosafot, Sukkah 36a; in most versions the text here reads: "like a sphere").
when it splits. When it divides.
when the breasts droop. When they grow somewhat and slope downward.
when the breasts shake. When they move as she walks.
and when it becomes stiff. When the hairs become stiff.
the swollen. The protruding.
we do not pay attention to it. We do not take it into account.
the lower sign. As above in halakhah 2.

for it is impossible for all of them to come unless the lower sign had already come and fallen out. It is not possible for the signs to come unless the lower sign also came, and now it is not visible because it fell out.
children are like signs. Giving birth is like a definitive sign of adulthood.
in the places known for hair. The pubic area (explained below in halakhot 16-17).
a saris. One whose sexual development is defective (for his signs see below halakhah 13).
and grew two hairs in the beard... he is not a saris. For hairs generally indicate that he is not a saris.
and his flesh is smooth. His skin is smooth and without hair.
foam. Froth.
and when he urinates he does not form an arch. A stream like a bow.
and his semen is thin. Its color is dark (ibid.).
and his urine does not ferment. It does not stink.
vapor. Steam.
a saris of the sun. A saris from birth.
that was cut or severed, etc. He was castrated by people in his childhood, and because of this injury the development of his body was impaired as he grew.
as the gentiles do. For this is forbidden to Israel (Hilchot Issurei Biah 16:10-11).
for this one never brings a sign. And therefore age alone determines.
the signs above. The hairs of the beard and the other signs mentioned above in halakhah 13.
so that its head can be bent to its root. That the tip of the hair can be bent toward its root.
to be cut by the mouth of the scissors. To be cut at the edge of the scissors.
and that there be pits at their roots. That the root of the hair comes out of a pit.
as we have explained. Above halakhah 1.
and in valuations. Vows whose rates are fixed and depend on the age of the person valued (for more detail see Hilchot Arakhin VeCharamin 1:2-4).
lunar years. Twelve lunar months, which are about 354 days (see Hilchot Kiddush HaChodesh 6:4).
solar years. Which are 365 days and six hours (ibid.).
but years of the order of intercalation, etc. Full years, from a certain date to the same date in the following year.
as we have explained in Hilchot Kiddush HaChodesh. Chapter 4 (and see 6:10-11 there).
we do not rely on women. Because they are disqualified from testimony (Hilchot Edut 9:2), and likewise relatives (ibid. 13:1).
a girl of three years and one day. From this age they are fit for relations (Hilchot Issurei Biah 1:13-14).

for an offering. If they transgressed a forbidden relation with an adult, the father is believed to obligate the adult to bring an offering, if it was unintentional (for the obligation see Hilchot Issurei Biah 1:1 and elsewhere).
but not for lashes or punishments. He is not believed to obligate him to lashes or the death penalty, for he is a single witness and the Torah did not trust him for this (see further ibid. 18:24).

for vows, valuations, consecrations and dedications. Vows of various kinds. A father is believed to say that his children are adults and their vow is a valid vow, even without checking whether they know in whose name they vowed (see Hilchot Nedarim 11:1-5).
but not for lashes or punishments. For if the children committed a transgression that carries a punishment, they are not held to be adults on the father's testimony.
but a closed one... a tumtum. His sexual organs are covered. [Note: Rambam in the Commentary on the Mishnah vocalizes this word: tumtom.]
and let them not depart from your eyes. Let them not leave your memory (based on Proverbs 3:21).

no less than a perutah of silver. The value of a perutah is refined silver weighing half a barleycorn (Hilchot Shekalim 1:3), and less than this is not considered money for any matter in the Torah (see for example Hilchot Genevah 1:1).
language of transfer. Words that mean acquisition.
betrothed by doubt. For the law of doubtful betrothal see below 4:6.
he writes on paper or on a potsherd, etc. On all of these a get may be written (Hilchot Gerushin 4:3), from which the law of a betrothal document is learned.
like a get. Just as a get must be written for the sake of the woman being divorced (see Hilchot Gerushin 3:1-7).
with her consent. With her knowledge, with her agreement.

and is alone with her before witnesses and has relations with her. The man is alone with the woman and has relations with her, while the witnesses are outside that place and testify that they saw them shut in there for a length of time that allows marital relations.
completion of relations. Insertion of the entire organ (Hilchot Issurei Biah 1:10).
not in her natural way. Relations through the rectum, from behind.
zekukah. Bound, from the root of zikah and bond.
my taken one. Acquired, in the language of the verse: "when a man takes a wife" (Deuteronomy 22:13).
my designated one. Set aside and specified, in the language of the verse: "and she is a maidservant designated to a man" (Leviticus 19:20).

you are my help, you are opposite me, you are my rib, you are my enclosed one, you are beneath me. These words are taken from the verses that describe the woman's purpose as a help for man, and her creation from one of his ribs: "I will make him a help opposite him... and He took one of his ribs and closed up the flesh in its place" (Genesis 2:18-21).
you are my bound one, you are my seized one. Words whose meaning is binding and holding.

and provided he is speaking with her about matters of betrothal. They spoke to one another about their wedding matters, and there is reason to suspect that he indeed meant those words for betrothal (as below halakhah 8).
we do not worry about these words. For they have no clear meaning of betrothal.
and a man may betroth a woman in any language she is familiar with. He may betroth in any language the woman understands.
as we have explained. Above halakhah 6.
and she agreed. She agreed to be betrothed.

since they are engaged in the matter, it is enough. He need not say explicitly that he is giving for the sake of betrothal, for from the context it can be understood that he is giving for betrothal (for a similar law regarding a get see Hilchot Gerushin 1:11).
he does not need to say to them, you are my witnesses. Unlike the rules in monetary cases, where this language must be used to define the testimony (see for example Hilchot Toen VeNitan 6:6).
to what is this similar... you are my wife and another. As if he said that he intends to add and betroth another woman, and so there is language of betrothal here.

he said to her, half of you is betrothed to me for a perutah and half of you for a perutah... half of you is betrothed to me for half a perutah and the other half for half a perutah, etc. In these two cases the halves he used in his speech are seen as a division of no significance, since in the end they combine with each other, and therefore she is betrothed.
half of you is betrothed to me for a perutah today, etc. Here there is a doubt whether the splitting into days prevents the halves from combining (see Kiddushin 7b).
your two halves for a perutah. Here there is a doubt whether the halves combine, since they were not acquired as additions to one another but together in divided form.
your two daughters... in all these she is betrothed by doubt. For there is doubt whether these were betrothals with a full perutah.
without her consent. Even without her agreement.
and her betrothal money belongs to her father. The father receives the betrothal money for himself.
and likewise he is entitled to what she finds. If she found a lost object, the find belongs to the father (Hilchot Gezelah VaAvedah 17:13).
and to the work of her hands. The profit from her labor belongs to the father.

and to her ketubah if she was divorced or widowed from betrothal. The ketubah is money the husband obligates himself to give her if he divorces her or dies (see below 10:7). If the betrothed wrote her a ketubah and died or divorced her (see ibid. halakhah 11), the money belongs to the father because she has not yet left his authority through marriage (below halakhah 12).
until she reaches majority. Until she is an adult (for the definition see above 2:2).
a deaf woman. For her definition see above 2:26.
even if she was deaf or insane, etc. Because they cannot betroth themselves by Torah-law betrothal (below 4:9).
a girl of three years and one day. For less than this age she is not fit for relations (Hilchot Issurei Biah 1:13).
her father betrothed her by relations. He handed her over for the sake of relations.
she consented. She agreed.

she is not forbidden to a priest. She is not like a divorcee, who is forbidden to an ordinary priest, or a widow, who is forbidden to a high priest (above 1:7), for there was no betrothal in the first place.
and both she and her father can prevent it. Cancel the betrothal; and even though she wanted it at first, she may change her mind.
whether she was betrothed in his presence, etc. Even if she was betrothed in his presence, this is not proof that he agreed to it unless he said so explicitly (see Hilchot Terumot 8:16).
a doubtful adult. When it is not known whether six months have passed since she reached the age of twelve years and a day.
a man may appoint an agent, etc. A person may appoint another to betroth on his behalf.
whether a particular woman or a woman from the rest of the women. He may appoint him to betroth a specific woman, and he may also appoint him to betroth any woman at the agent's discretion.
anyone who appoints an agent to receive the betrothal. A father for his daughter's betrothal and a woman for her own betrothal.

must appoint him before two witnesses. Just as betrothal must be done before witnesses (above halakhah 1), so too this agency, because by the agent's receiving the betrothal the woman's status changes (see Yad Peshutah, and see also Hilchot Gerushin 6:1).

for there is no place for witnesses in the man's agency except to make known the truth of the matter. The need for witnesses regarding an agent to betroth is only as evidence of the appointment, and they are not needed for the validity of the appointment.
the agent for a get. Appointed by the husband or the wife to transfer the get from the husband to the wife (ibid. 6:3-4).
an agent who was authorized to separate terumah for him. A person who appointed an agent to separate terumah for him from his produce (Hilchot Terumot 4:1, and see below halakhah 17).

the agent becomes a witness. And we do not say that since the agent is like the principal, just as the principal himself is not believed to testify in a matter touching himself, so too his agent does not testify.

and it says, so you too shall separate, etc. Regarding the separation of terumot and tithes. From the word "too" they learned that a person's agent too may separate terumah from the grain for him. And from the law of agency for separating terumah, the law of agency in the whole Torah is learned (Hilchot Sheluchin VeShutafin 2:1).

a slave, although he can become an agent, etc. A Canaanite slave who was circumcised and immersed for the sake of slavery is obligated in the commandments like a woman (Hilchot Issurei Biah 12:11, Hilchot Chagigah 2:1), and in this respect he is a member of the covenant and can be an agent in a monetary matter. But the laws of betrothal and divorce do not apply to him, and therefore he cannot be an agent in them (below 4:15, Hilchot Gerushin 3:16).
yes. Yes.
they were engaged in the matter. Speaking about matters of betrothal (as above halakhah 8).
and he gave to the father or to the agent. The betrothal money.
it is enough. As with one who gives to the woman, above halakhah 8.
with the knowledge of the father or the knowledge of the agent. As with one who gives a document to the woman, above halakhah 4.

it is a commandment that a man betroth his wife himself, etc. Although the betrothal takes effect in any case, it is proper that the commandment be done by him and not by an agent (for a similar law see Hilchot Shabbat 30:6).
until she grows up and says, I want so-and-so. So that the marriage will be of her own will (and see further Hilchot Issurei Biah 21:25).
and he shall not betroth a woman until he has seen her and she is acceptable in his eyes. It is proper to look at her face to see whether she is pleasing to him (ibid. 21:3).
or lies with her while he hates her. And this is forbidden (ibid. 21:12).
just as he completes and divorces... so he completes and brings in. Just as a get document creates a complete divorce, so a betrothal document creates a full acquisition.

money is Torah law, and its interpretation is rabbinic. Betrothal by money is valid by Torah law like betrothal by document or relations, except that it is not explicitly mentioned in the Torah and was learned by the Sages (Yad Peshutah). This is the text of the final edition that Rambam wrote; at first it read: "but money is rabbinic," and see above 1:2.

as it says, I have given the money of the field, take it from me. These are the words of Abraham to Ephron the Hittite, in the negotiations they conducted over the sale of the Cave of Machpelah. From a gezerah shavah (verbal analogy) on the term "taking," the Sages learned that a woman's acquisition too is by money.
lashes for rebellion. Lashes by rabbinic enactment.
without shiduch. Without prior agreement between the man and woman or between the families concerning the marriage.
one who betroths in the market. In a public place.
and be likened to a kedeshah. To harlotry (as above 1:4).
as blessings are said before all the commandments. Before performing them (Hilchot Berakhot 11:2).

and if he betrothed and did not bless, he does not bless after the betrothal... what was done was done. For betrothal is an act whose performance is already completed, and one does not bless after it (see ibid. 11:5).
and forbade us the betrothed women. For the betrothed woman is forbidden to her husband by rabbinic enactment until she enters the chuppah (below 10:1).
chuppah and betrothal. Marriage that was preceded by betrothal (above 1:1).
who was forced. Who was compelled.
and a man may betroth many women at once. A man may betroth several women at one time.

and one of them or another may receive the betrothal for all of them with their consent. It is possible that one of the women, or another agent, receives the betrothal money all at once for all of them with their agreement.
and gave her betrothal money with her consent into the hand of her friend. The friend became an agent for her.
too. Also.

and therefore she accepted the betrothal, for he is still asking her to see what is in her heart. It is possible that she accepted the betrothal thinking that he is asking her and is not betrothing her.
to the fire. To fire, and it was burned.

to a thing that will be lost, etc. To a place where the betrothal money will be destroyed, which shows that she does not want the betrothal. She said to him, give it to my father... she is not betrothed. For by saying that he should give it to another, it is understood that she does not want the betrothal.
that he receive it for me, and he gave, she is betrothed. For she explicitly agreed.

and if it was her sela, she is betrothed. For if he throws onto her sela, she acquires the denar by the law of acquisition by courtyard (Hilchot Zekhiyah UMatanah 4:8), and from this it is understood that she agreed to the betrothal.

if the sela belonged to both of them, she is betrothed by doubt. Since there is doubt whether she acquires in a shared place (see below halakhah 21), it is not clear whether she agreed to the betrothal or not.
in a loaf. A loaf of bread.
even if it was a poor person whom she supports, she is not betrothed. Even if she ordinarily supports that poor person, she is not betrothed, for she received no benefit from the man.
and if it was her dog, she is betrothed. For she benefits from it.
he was running after her to bite her... she is betrothed by doubt. Although she benefited from being saved from the bite, there is doubt whether she intended to be betrothed to him by this benefit.
even though both admit. That the man and woman say that he betrothed her, because betrothal takes effect only with two valid witnesses (see Hilchot Gerushin 1:13).
one who betroths with witnesses disqualified by the Torah, etc. The witnesses of the betrothal were disqualified from testifying by Torah law or by rabbinic law (see Hilchot Edut chapters 9-10).
to marry. In marriage.

she needs a get from him out of doubt. Perhaps the betrothal took effect (and see Yad Peshutah, who explained why with those disqualified by rabbinic law she needs a get out of doubt and not for certain).
a minor. Under the age of thirteen (above 2:10).
but an adult who betrothed, etc. For a similar law see Hilchot Gerushin 11:7.
or a minor girl who left her father's authority. Whom her father married off and who afterward was divorced or widowed (above 3:12), and she is in her own authority like an orphan.
clever in whispering. Wise.
and recognizes and discerns. Understands the matters.
foolish. Silly.
the beauty of her understanding. The degree of her understanding.
she must refuse before two, etc. And thereby cancels her marriage to that man.
as will be explained in Hilchot Gerushin. 11:8.
she stayed with her husband until she grew up, her betrothal is complete. If her husband had relations with her after she reached the age of na'arut (Hilchot Gerushin 11:6).
a deaf man. For his definition see above 2:26.
and she is permitted to her deaf husband. And we do not suspect that people will say, "he took back his divorcee after she was betrothed to another" (Lechem Mishneh).
there is no betrothal here at all. For the Sages did not enact marriage with an insane person, because "a person of sound mind cannot live in one house with the insane" (Hilchot Gerushin 10:23).
a saris... an aylonit. For their definitions see above chapter 2.
doubtful betrothal. Because they are doubtfully male and doubtfully female (see above 2:24-25).
the forbidden relations. See above 1:5.
and it is not proper to do so. Because she is not fit for relations and chuppah, but one must wait until she becomes pure (for the law of marrying a niddah see below 10:2).
who extended. Held out.
she is betrothed to the second, for the woman who said, etc. For accepting betrothal from another man in front of her husband is like a claim that he divorced her earlier.

a presumption: she does not brazenly lie in front of her husband. A woman does not have the audacity to lie to his face in this matter, and if she claims so, he surely divorced her (see Hilchot Gerushin 12:4).
the secondary relations... from prohibitions of negative commandments... from prohibitions of positive commandments. Those detailed above 1:6-8.

the co-wife of a yevamah. When one of the dead man's wives was taken in yibbum, and therefore her co-wives became forbidden to the brothers by a positive-commandment prohibition (Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 1:12).

except a yevamah who was betrothed to a stranger, who is betrothed by doubt, etc. A woman bound to yibbum whom a man other than the dead man's brother betrothed. From what is stated in the Torah, "the wife of the deceased shall not be outside to a strange man" (Deuteronomy 25:5), it is not decided whether this is a definition of her status - that she cannot be betrothed to another man - or a prohibition of a negative commandment, and betrothal takes effect on her (and for her law see Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 2:18).
a maidservant. A Canaanite maidservant.
but after betrothal she is as she was before betrothal. There is no marital connection between them at all, and she is in any case forbidden to an Israelite (Hilchot Issurei Biah chapter 12).
an Israelite apostate. A Jew who converted out of his religion.
a woman who is half maidservant and half free. A maidservant who belonged to two masters, and one of them freed his portion in her (Hilchot Avadim 7:4).
is not betrothed with a complete betrothal. For the betrothal does not take effect on the part in which she is still a maidservant.
her betrothal is completed like the betrothal of a minor who grew up. For if her husband had relations with her after she was freed, her betrothal is completed (see above halakhah 8).

another came and betrothed her after she was freed, it is a doubtful betrothal for both. For it was not decided whether her being freed suffices to complete the betrothal, or whether relations are needed as well (Yad Peshutah).

and which is the designated maidservant mentioned in the Torah. "And if a man lies carnally with a woman, and she is a maidservant designated to a man..." (Leviticus 19:20-22), where one who has relations with her brings a special guilt offering (see Hilchot Issurei Biah 3:13-17).

this is one who is half maidservant and half free, whom a Hebrew slave betrothed. He is permitted even to a Canaanite maidservant (Hilchot Avadim 3:3). This law was brought to show that betrothal applies to a half-maidservant, half-free woman, and is completed when she is freed (Yad Peshutah).

and if he reached the drunkenness of Lot, his betrothal is not betrothal. For if he got so drunk that he is not aware of his actions at all, his acts and words have no force (see Hilchot Mekhirah 29:18).
and they investigate this matter. They examine carefully the circumstances of the case and the degree of his drunkenness (Yad Peshutah).
one who betroths with less than a perutah, she is not betrothed. For less than a perutah is not considered money (see above 3:1).

one who betroths a woman with less than a perutah... even if he sent gifts afterward, she is not betrothed. Even if he sent her gifts after the betrothal (see below 9:28), and they are worth more than a perutah, she is not betrothed (and for the law of relations after betrothal with less than a perutah see below 7:23). Because those people, who at first betrothed invalidly, sent the gifts on the basis of the first betrothal, which was invalid, and did not intend to betroth her with them.
and threw them into her hand, or into her lap, or into her courtyard, etc. In all of these she acquires the object (and the same applies to a get, see Hilchot Gerushin 5:1).

she was standing in the husband's domain, etc. If she is in a place belonging to the husband, the money or document must actually reach her, and not merely rest on the ground near her (and see ibid. 5:8).
with her consent. By her wish and agreement to be betrothed.
these are doubtful betrothals. For there is doubt whether she acquires in a domain shared by both (see above halakhah 4).

they were standing in a public domain or in a domain that belongs to neither of them, etc. She can acquire even if the betrothal money lies in a domain that is not hers, if it is close to where she stands (for a similar law regarding a get see Hilchot Gerushin 5:13-15).
and they were lost before reaching her hand. So that it is impossible to check which of them it was near.
how is it near her and near him, etc. The rule is that it does not depend only on the measured distance between them, but on the ability to guard the object.
with something forbidden for benefit. With an object from which all use is forbidden (and not only eating).
such as chametz on Pesach or meat cooked in milk. Which are forbidden to eat and to derive any benefit from by Torah law (see Hilchot Chametz UMatzah 1:2, Hilchot Maachalot Asurot 9:1).

and even if it was forbidden for benefit by rabbinic law, such as chametz in the sixth hour of the fourteenth. For chametz is forbidden for benefit by Torah law from midday on the fourteenth of Nisan, which is the end of the sixth hour. And by rabbinic law it is forbidden to benefit from it from the beginning of the sixth hour (Hilchot Chametz UMatzah 1:8-9).
she is not betrothed. For she did not receive anything she can benefit from.

he transgressed and sold something forbidden for benefit and betrothed with its proceeds. Although the thing is forbidden for any use, including sale, the money given in exchange for it was not forbidden for benefit, and he may betroth with it.
for the proceeds of idolatry are forbidden for benefit like itself. The prohibition applies even to money given in exchange for it (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 7:9).
with the dung of idolatrous calves. Waste in the intestines of animals offered to idolatry (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 7:3).

an ox to be stoned. An ox condemned to stoning, for example because it killed a person (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 10:1), whose flesh is forbidden for benefit even if it was slaughtered (Hilchot Maachalot Asurot 4:22).
with produce of the Sabbatical year. Produce that grew in the Sabbatical year, in which trading is forbidden (Hilchot Shemitah VeYovel 6:1).

or with the ashes of a red heifer or with water that he filled to make them niddah-waters. With ashes from the burning of a red heifer, or with water mixed with the ashes of the red heifer, to sprinkle on one defiled by a corpse to purify him from his impurity. It is forbidden to take payment for sprinkling the ashes of the heifer on the impure, or for mixing the ashes into water.
she is betrothed. Because it is possible to receive payment for them in certain ways.
with a consecrated item for the upkeep of the Temple. Money or property dedicated to the Temple.

unintentionally, she is betrothed. For he did not know that it was consecrated, and the law is that he committed me'ilah (misuse of consecrated property), and the consecrated item became ordinary, and it turns out he betroths with his own property (Hilchot Me'ilah 6:3).
as is the law of anyone who commits me'ilah unintentionally. Ibid. 1:3.
intentionally, she is not betrothed. For there is no me'ilah here, and the property remains in the ownership of the consecrated fund.

with second tithe. One of the tithes of the produce of the Land of Israel, which the owners eat in Jerusalem in purity, or redeem with money ("desanctify"), and eat the proceeds there (Hilchot Maaser Sheni chapters 2-4).
for he may not do with it his other affairs until it is redeemed. The produce is as if belonging to God, and it is forbidden to use it until it is redeemed and made ordinary (ibid. 3:17).

a priest who betrothed with his portion of the most holy offerings, etc. Who took the portion he received to eat from the offerings of high or lesser holiness (see Hilchot Maaseh HaKorbanot 10:14 ff.), and betrothed a woman with it.
for they were permitted only for eating. For this purpose they were given to the priests, and not to be as their property.

with terumah gedolah and terumat maaser, etc. For all these are parts of the crop given to priests, Levites and the poor (for the order of their separation see Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 6:1-6), and they are considered property of the recipient in every respect.

gifts that were not yet taken up are as if they were taken up. Even if terumot and tithes have not yet been separated from the grain, for several purposes it is considered as if they had already been separated.

an Israelite who inherited tevel from his mother's father's house, who was a priest. An Israelite received by inheritance from his grandfather, who was a priest, produce from which terumot and tithes had not been separated.

they are like terumot and tithes that fell to him by inheritance from his mother's father. They are treated like terumot and tithes inherited from the grandfather after being separated, and they are the grandson's property.
for even though it is not fit for him to eat, etc. Although terumah is forbidden to an Israelite to eat, he has a right in it, for he can sell it to priests.
with terumah that he separated from his threshing floor. That he must give to priests.

for he may not sell it and has in it only the benefit of choosing... and the benefit of choosing is not money. He is forbidden to sell it to priests, and the only right he has in terumah is the ability to give it to a particular priest ("benefit of choosing"), and this right is not considered as having monetary value.
by robbery. Property acquired against the will of the seller (Hilchot Mekhirah 10:5).

and it became known that he had acquired that thing by despair. For the owners' despair of getting the object back in certain cases acquires the object for the robber, although he is obligated to return its value (for the manner of acquisition see Hilchot Genevah 5:3, Hilchot Gezelah 2:3). Eighth: So as not to be embarrassed with him. The householder said this so as not to embarrass the buyer, but did not truly mean it.
with something about which the householder is not particular. Which is of little value, and the householder gladly forgoes it.
there was merchandise between him and his friend. That two were partners in merchandise.
court valuation. An appraisal of value by experts.
for this one does not take for himself what he wants and leave what he wants. He may not divide jointly owned property without agreement or appraisal (see Hilchot Sheluchin VeShutafin 5:9).

if there was a shiduch between them beforehand and she took it and was silent, she is betrothed. If there was prior agreement about their marriage, her silence is interpreted as consent, for she is about to be betrothed to him.
and if she said yes, she is betrothed. If she said so, she agreed to be betrothed with this object even though it belonged to her and was robbed from her.
for any silence after the giving of money is of no effect. After the money is already in her hand, silence is not interpreted as consent.
take in this deposit. Take it to guard it for me.

if he said to her before she took it, and she took it and was silent, she is betrothed. For she took the deposit after he told her it was for betrothal, and from her taking it, it is understood that she agreed to the betrothal.
a debt she had with him. That he owed her money.
if there was a shiduch between them, she is betrothed. As above in halakhah 10.
one who betroths with a loan. Who forgave her a debt she owed him, and wants her to be betrothed to him in exchange.
for whom he had a debt of a denar with her. That she owed him a denar.
for a loan was given to be spent, etc. The loan was meant for the borrower to use the money, and he gave her no benefit by forgiving the debt.
a loan on a pledge. That she borrowed money and gave an object as security for repaying her debt.
with the benefit of the time that I will grant you. That the money will be in your hands for a certain time, and I will not claim it from you during that time.
because it is like interest. For the lender gains something additional from the loan, which is the betrothal.
and my teachers explained the benefit of a loan in ways that are not fit to be heard. That is, they said in this regard interpretations that are not correct (see Piskei VeShitot).
and with the debt that I have with you. That I will forgive you what you owe me.
she is betrothed. For there is a perutah that is not a loan, and so it turns out she received from him something she benefits from.
and likewise if he said to her, with the loan that I have with you and with a perutah. It makes no difference whether he mentioned the debt or the perutah first.

with the debt I have in this man's hand, in the presence of the three of them. With money that another person owes me. If the man, the woman and the debtor are present together, the right to collect the debt passes from him to her (see Hilchot Mekhirah 6:8).
she is betrothed. With the right to collect the debt.
he betrothed her with a deposit that he has in her hands or a loan that he lent her. That he deposited or lent her an object, and he betroths her with it.
and the ruler left her alone and did not claim from her. The ruler did not collect money from her, because of the man's intercession.

for the benefit that came to her from his words is like a loan. For this is a kind of wage for work, and if he forgoes the payment, it turns out that he betroths her with a loan (see in the next halakhah).
with this work that I will do with you. That I will do for you.
for the worker acquires wages from the beginning to the end. For every part of the work he is immediately entitled to payment, which accumulates as a debt of the employer.
that I gave at your word. That I gave at your command.
an important person. A distinguished person.
and he did not give the pledge to be hers. He gave it only to secure payment of his obligation.
he has some ownership in the body of the pledge. For some purposes the pledge is considered his (see Hilchot Sekhirut 10:1).
a bundle. A package, a bunch.
for silence after money is placed in her hand is of no effect. It is not considered consent (above halakhah 11).
lest it be worth a perutah in another place. As above 4:19.
with a date. With the fruit of the date palm.
be betrothed to me with this. And each time he gave her another date.
if one of them is worth a perutah. For the dates do not combine with one another, since he used the language of betrothal with each one.
if all of them together are worth a perutah, she is betrothed. For from his wording it is understood that he intended to betroth her with all of them together.
she is betrothed only by doubt. Perhaps they are worth a perutah in another country.
she ate each one as she received it. She ate immediately each date that came into her hand.
they are like a loan. Like a debt she owes him, which in the end he forgave.
and one who betroths with a loan, she is not betrothed. Above halakhah 13.
you are betrothed to me with these. With these dates.
she eats what is hers. For from the beginning the dates were combined, and since she received them as betrothal money, they are her property and are not like a loan.
water... it and what is in it. The cup and the water combine to be worth a perutah.
wine... it and not what is in it. Only in the cup itself, and not the wine in it.
oil... what is in it and not it. In the oil and not the cup.
and we do not pay attention to the cup. We do not count the cup's value.
whether the condition was from the man or from the woman. Each of them has the ability to impose a condition on the betrothal.

and every condition in the world... the condition must have four things. See evidence that the rules of conditions apply to all laws, below halakhah 14. The laws of conditions in divorce are explained in Hilchot Gerushin chapters 8-9, their laws in buying and selling in Hilchot Mekhirah chapter 11, and their laws in other monetary matters in Hilchot Zekhiyah UMatanah 3:7-8.
that it be a doubled condition. Explained below in halakhah 3.
and that its yes precede its no. Explained below in halakhah 6.
and that the condition precede the act. Explained below in halakhah 4.
and that the condition be something possible to fulfill. Explained below in halakhah 7.
the condition stands. It is valid.

even though everything is within the time of a speech. Even if the condition was stated within the length of time it takes to say "Peace upon you, my teacher" (Hilchot Shevuot 2:17) after the words of betrothal, it is not valid.
for it is known that she cannot fulfill this condition. Therefore the condition is void and the act takes effect immediately.
this is only like one who exaggerates in words by way of jest and mockery. His speech is not serious.
and we do not say here that he stipulated against what is written in the Torah. For in such a case the law is that his condition is void (as explained in the next halakhah).

anyone who stipulates against what is written in the Torah, his condition is void, except in a monetary matter. Only in matters concerning monetary law can the two sides agree on conduct that is not according to Torah law (see below 12:9).
your condition is void and your acts have been established. The act takes full effect, independent of the condition.

on the condition that she has no claim on him for food, clothing and conjugal rights. That he betroths her on the condition that he be exempt from supplying her food and clothing and from having marital relations with her, which are things he obligated himself to by Torah law when he married her (below 12:2).

a beautiful woman (yefat to'ar). Whom the Torah permitted a soldier to take from the captives of war, a gentile woman he desires, and to have relations with her, and to marry her after she converts (see Hilchot Melakhim chapter 8).
that he may treat her as a slave. That he will use her as a maidservant, which is forbidden by the Torah (ibid. 8:6).
for it is not in her power to make others transgress. She cannot cause others to commit a transgression.
with the other four things. Which were discussed in detail from the beginning of the chapter until here.

from the conditions of the children of Reuben and the children of Gad. Moses our teacher stipulated with these tribes that if they would help the other tribes in the war of conquering the land they would inherit across the Jordan, and if not they would receive an inheritance in the Land of Canaan like the other tribes.
and so too is the law in divorces. See Hilchot Gerushin 8:1, 9:5.
and in monetary matters. Hilchot Mekhirah 11:1, Hilchot Zekhiyah UMatanah 3:6.
betrothed retroactively. From the time of the act of betrothal, and not from the time the condition is fulfilled.

anyone who says "from now" need not double his condition, etc. For stipulating "from now" binds the act and the condition together, and gives the condition extra force to cancel the act (Rosh, Gittin 6:15, citing the Ra'avad). Some suggested that the need for detailed wording according to the rules of conditions arises from the fact that the time the act takes effect is postponed until the condition is fulfilled (Yad Peshutah).
or was silent... she is not betrothed. For he did not agree when he heard.
that he not protest. That he not object.
we teach the father. We instruct him to protest the betrothal in order to cancel it from the outset, thereby exempting the woman from the need for yibbum or chalitzah.
with this. With what he gives her for betrothal.
a beit kor of earth. A field fit for sowing a kor of grain.
in order to ruin her. To cause her a mishap, that she marry another man in transgression.
and he shall show her. And he must show her in order for the condition to be fulfilled.
she is not betrothed until he shows her from his own. Property that belongs to him.
as a sharecropper. A sharecropper is one who receives a field to work in exchange for a certain percentage of the crop.
for it implies, "I will show you what I have for myself, this thing I told you". That the expression "until I show you" means he will show her property or assets that belong entirely to him.
crevices. Clefts.
and they are not measured with it. They are not counted as part of the measure of the beit kor.
one of these three vows, etc. Which a person is usually particular about, because they are vows of self-affliction or vows that harm the relationship between him and her (Hilchot Nedarim 12:1-3).
in kinds of colored items. Cosmetics or colored clothing.
even if it turns out that she vowed not to eat carobs. An example of a vow of no importance, but that person revealed his opinion that he wants no vow at all.
even though he said, I am particular... she is betrothed. Because most people are not particular about them.
those that disqualify among priests. From service in the Temple.
and in Hilchot Biat HaMikdash. Chapters 7-8.
and breasts larger than her companions'. Breasts larger than those of other women.
and a mole on the forehead. A wart on the forehead.
even if close to the hair of her head. So that it is not very prominent.
and even though there is no hair on it. Even if no hairs grew on the mole, it disqualifies in women.
and this is the mole that is additional in a woman over priests. It is a blemish that disqualifies women and not priests.
like an issar. A small coin.
one who betroths a woman without specification. Without stipulating that she have no vows or blemishes.
one of three vows. Mentioned above in halakhah 6.
she is betrothed by doubt. Perhaps a person does not want a woman who makes vows or has blemishes, even if he did not say so explicitly.
and she went to a sage and he released her. The sage can release her from her vow when she regrets it (see Hilchot Nedarim 4:5, Hilchot Shevuot chapter 6).

she is betrothed. Because she has no vows now, and there is no disgrace in vows she made in the past and which were released. Ninth: And she had blemishes and went to a physician and he healed her, she is not betrothed, etc. Because the man is particular about blemishes that a woman has, and it is distasteful to him even if they were healed. But in the opposite case the woman is not particular.
after thirty days. That the betrothal take effect in thirty days.
that were consumed. The woman spent the money and it is no longer in her possession.
she is betrothed. For she received money for the sake of betrothal.
and if he retracted within the thirty days or she retracted, she is not betrothed. Because the betrothal had not yet taken effect.
when the first betrothal comes into effect, it will find her a married woman. At the time when the first betrothal is due to take effect, it turns out that she is already married to the second.
for betrothal does not take effect on her. For betrothal does not take effect on a forbidden relation (above 4:12).
betrothed by doubt to both. Because there is doubt whether the first man's betrothal takes effect from now or only after thirty days.

for he stipulated something impossible to fulfill. For a woman cannot be betrothed to two men (above 3:9), and therefore the condition is void. But when he said "except for so-and-so," he limited the betrothal not by way of a condition, and therefore there is doubt whether it works.
and when he divorces her she will be betrothed. Based on what he said when he first betrothed her, she will be betrothed with the second perutah after the divorce.
after I convert, after you convert. That the betrothal is made while one of the parties is still a gentile.

after I am freed, after you are freed. That the betrothal is made when one of the parties is a Canaanite slave, who is not subject to the law of betrothal (above 4:15), and after being freed will be permitted to marry an Israelite (Hilchot Issurei Biah 13:12).
after your sister dies. It speaks of the sister of his wife, who is forbidden to him while his wife is alive, and after his wife's death is permitted to him (ibid. 2:9).
betrothal took effect on her by doubt. As explained above 4:14.
your wife, a female child, is betrothed to me. If a daughter is born to you, that daughter is betrothed to me.
he said nothing. There is no betrothal here at all, for there is no one here who can be betrothed.
and if his friend's wife was pregnant and the fetus was recognizable. It was visible to onlookers that she is pregnant.

so that he may marry her in betrothals that have no blemish. With betrothals that have no deficiency. The ruling here that she is betrothed is stated out of stringency, but by law a person cannot transfer something not yet in the world, nor transfer to one not yet in the world (Hilchot Mekhirah 22:10), so it turns out there was no betrothal here (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kiddushin 3:5).
and he will complete the rest for her. On condition that he complete the full sum he undertook.
she is not betrothed until he completes. Until he gives all that he said.
to retract from one another. To regret.
and likewise if a maneh was found lacking a denar. It became clear that in the hundred denarii he told her about, one was missing.
a copper denar. And not silver, as it should have been.

a bad denar was found among them; if she can spend it with difficulty, he exchanges it. If one of the coins is flawed, then if there are merchants willing to accept it, it can still be treated as a denar, and there is a maneh and she is betrothed. But the man must replace it with a currently circulating denar.
and if not, she is not betrothed. If the coin cannot be spent even with difficulty.
and they need no market appraisal... so that she will rely. There is no need to appraise the clothes' price in advance, in order to make the woman believe they are worth what he told her.
and this one went to his home and that one to hers. Without agreement.
they sued one another and betrothed without specification. They expressed the wish to marry, and he betrothed her without mentioning the sum.
the woman's words are carried out. He must complete the rest as the woman wanted (see above halakhah 17).
and the agent went and betrothed her on condition, she is not betrothed. For he did not fulfill his mission as required (see Hilchot Sheluchin VeShutafin 1:2).
betroth her for me in such-and-such place, etc. In this case it appears that the sender wants the betrothal to be done in that specific place, and the agent deviated from his mission.

and she is in such-and-such place... for it is pointing out the place to him. In this case the place is mentioned only so that the agent knows where to find her, and the sender is not particular about it.

and he retracted immediately... within the time of a speech their retraction is nothing and she is betrothed. Even if they retracted within the length of time it takes to say "Peace upon you, my teacher" (Hilchot Shevuot 2:17) from the betrothal, the retraction is of no use. And although ordinarily a retraction within speech cancels the earlier statement, in betrothal this rule is not valid (Bava Batra 129b).
for she relied on this relations. That it be for the sake of betrothal.
and it was found to be of honey. After she accepted the betrothal she discovered that he had misled her.
a Nathin. See above 1:7 in the explanation.
a resident of a large city. A resident of a major city.
a daughter or maidservant who braids hair or bakes. That he has a daughter or maidservant who has a trade, braiding hair or baking.
she is not betrothed. For he stipulated that she be betrothed specifically on this condition.
things in the heart are not things. What was not said explicitly has no force (for another application of the rule see Hilchot Mekhirah 11:9).
a spice seller. A seller of perfumes.
and a tanner. One who processes hides, whose smell is bad.
and his name turned out to be Joseph and Simeon. That some call him by one name and some by another.
that I know how to read. And it means: knows how to read the Torah.

that he reads the Torah and translates it with the translation of Onkelos the convert. It was customary to accompany the public reading of the Torah with an Aramaic translation (see Hilchot Tefillah 12:10-12). The translation of Onkelos is the accepted Aramaic translation in Israel, and is considered authoritative (see for example Hilchot Issurei Biah 12:13, Hilchot Evel 5:19).
a reader. Which means: expert in Scripture.
a tanna. Which means: expert in the collections of the Tannaim.
and Sifra and Sifrei. Collections of halakhic midrash, arranged on the books of Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy.
and the Tosefta of Rabbi Chiyya. A collection of halakhot of the Tannaim, which are a supplement to the Mishnah.
a student. A student of the Sages, a person occupied with Torah.
like Ben Azzai and Ben Zoma. Who were called students because they were not ordained, although they were among the greatest in Israel.
that they ask him one thing in his learning and he says it. That he knows how to answer questions on the subjects he studies.
like Abner son of Ner and Joab. Who were commanders of Israel's armies.
perhaps he reflected on repentance in his mind. And therefore now he is righteous.
lest your heart be seduced. Israel were warned not to let their hearts be seduced into idolatry.
in order to seize the house of Israel by their heart. That for this transgression, idolatry, they are punished ("seized") even for thoughts of the heart alone.
because they did not mislead him. Rather he erred on his own.
at once. Together.
a woman and her daughter or two sisters. Where by betrothing one of them the other becomes forbidden to him as a forbidden relation (Hilchot Issurei Biah 2:7, 2:9).
none of them is betrothed. Not one of them is betrothed to him, because betrothal does not take effect on forbidden relations (above 4:12), and this is a betrothal of a forbidden relation.
none of them all is betrothed. Since he included in his words women who are not betrothable because of forbidden relation, the betrothal is void for all of them.
the one of you fit for relations is betrothed to me, etc. He made the betrothal depend on the practical possibility of marrying them, and so did not include those who are forbidden to one another.
a maidservant or a gentile woman. On whom betrothal does not take effect (above 4:15).
through her friend. By the agency of the other.
and the father received her betrothal. For the father can betroth his daughter before she reaches majority (see above 3:11).
they need a get. In order to permit them to others.

and he is forbidden to have relations with either of them. Because each of them is possibly the sister of his wife, and is forbidden. Fourth: Both need a get and are forbidden to him. Even after he gave a get to one of them, for the prohibition of forbidden relations of kinship is not annulled after divorce (see Hilchot Issurei Biah 2:7-9).
one gives a get and one marries. For after she is divorced from one, she is permitted to marry the other.
among those who are distant. Who are not relatives.
for the presumption is that the agent carries out his mission. We assume the agent did what he was commanded.

four gets and a chalitzah from one of them. A get from each of the remaining brothers, lest she was betrothed to one of them, and chalitzah lest she was betrothed to the brother who died. And chalitzah from one of the brothers suffices to exempt all of them from the obligation of chalitzah (Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 1:9).
and the adult woman gave him permission to betroth her. Since she is no longer under his authority, he cannot betroth her unless she appointed him as her agent (above 3:11-12).
and he betrothed his daughter without specification to one man. He received the betrothal without clarifying for which of his daughters he received it.
the adult is not included. For by default he betrothed the minor daughter, since she is under his authority.
groups. Classes, categories.
in his authority. That he can betroth them without their knowledge.
the father is believed... before she reaches majority. Because at that time he still has the power to betroth her (above 3:11; and see Hilchot Issurei Biah 18:24).

he is believed even to marry. Not only is he believed regarding permitting her to others by a get (see below halakhah 14), where he gains nothing, but he is believed even if he wants to marry her, and we do not suspect that he lies out of desire to marry her, because he fears that the father will recognize that it was not he who betrothed her.
both give a get. Because both are believed equally.
he married her and afterward another came... he is not believed. For he is not believed to forbid a woman to her husband.

but he is not believed to marry, lest his inclination overcome him, etc. In such a case we suspect that he lies and says he betrothed her, and that the woman will cooperate with him even though it was not he who betrothed her, so that she not be forbidden to everyone (compare above halakhah 12). Therefore he is not believed except to permit her by a get.
he is forbidden to her relatives and she is permitted to his relatives. For a person can impose prohibitions on himself but not on others (see Hilchot Gerushin 12:3).
to her relatives. Who would be forbidden to him had he betrothed her with certain betrothal (see Hilchot Issurei Biah 2:7-9).
the adult. The mother.
and he is permitted to the daughter's relatives. For the mother is not believed regarding her daughter's betrothal.
who claim the betrothal. Who claimed there was betrothal, whether the man or the woman.
as we have explained. Above 4:6. In order to permit her to the rest of the people. For she says she is forbidden, because she is a married woman.
for he has no loss in this. He will suffer no monetary loss from writing the get (see Maggid Mishneh).
on his own. And not at the request of the court.
we compel him to give a ketubah. For it appears from his actions that he indeed betrothed her.
is called wicked. Because he acted deceitfully (Hilchot Mekhirah 7:10).

if the agent did not act with witnesses, etc. Since the agent was appointed without witnesses, he is believed to claim he betrothed for himself and not for the sender. But since the woman does not admit that she was betrothed to him, the law is as in the case where one side claims there was betrothal and the other denies (above halakhah 15).

and if the agent was established with witnesses, etc. Since he was appointed before witnesses and established as an agent, we assume he carried out his mission and betrothed for the sender (Bnei Ahuvah).

she said I do not know... if the agent was not established with witnesses, she is betrothed to the second. Since the agent was appointed without witnesses, he is believed to claim he betrothed for himself and not for the sender, and since the woman does not contradict him, she is betrothed to him.

and if he was established as his agent, both give a get, etc. From the fact that he was established as an agent we should assume he betrothed her to the first, as above; but since he claims he betrothed her for himself and the woman does not contradict him, she is doubtfully betrothed to both (Bnei Ahuvah).
who appointed an agent to betroth her. To receive her betrothal money on her behalf.
and leaves one ketubah between them and withdraws. For he owes only the money of one ketubah.
the Sages fined him. Because it is forbidden to betroth by relations at the outset (above 3:21; for a similar fine see Hilchot Gezelah 4:9).

and it is known that the ketubah he wrote, etc. It speaks here of a case where the one who betrothed wrote a ketubah to one of them and the ketubah was lost, for the obligation of ketubah from betrothal exists only if he wrote it for her (below 10:11).
was established. Was examined and found to be substantial.
the lamps are burning and the beds are spread, etc. Signs of betrothal celebration.
we do not worry about her. She is not presumed betrothed.
perhaps they were prepared to betroth and she was not betrothed. For it is possible that they prepared to betroth but in the end did not betroth.
a pretext. A justification and explanation for the act.
if the matters show the court that it is so. If it is apparent to the court that the pretext is true.
one writes a get and one marries. For the betrothals of both are equal.
to send sivlonot. Gifts the groom sends to the bride.
her ketubah document was established. It is known that he wrote her a ketubah.
we worry about her. That she was betrothed, and she needs a get if she wants to marry another man.

and even if there is no scribe there, etc. Even if there is no scribe in that place who writes documents, we do not explain the writing by saying that he feared he would not find a scribe later and wrote beforehand, but we worry about betrothal.
for "we did not see her" is no proof. Not seeing is meaningless in a matter done without publicity (see Hilchot Gerushin 12:8).
for she says, I was not betrothed. By marrying it is as if she said explicitly that she was not betrothed to another (Merkevet HaMishneh, and see above 4:13).
and we saw substance in her words. That she gave a convincing explanation.
the betrothed woman. A woman betrothed to a man.
by the words of the scribes. By rabbinic enactment.
lashes for rebellion. The punishment of lashes for one who transgresses the words of the Sages.
even if he betrothed her by relations. Which is one of the three ways of betrothal the Sages enumerated (above 1:2).
and one who has relations with his betrothed for the sake of marriage, etc. Even if he did not bring her into his house.

once he performs the act of beginning, he has acquired her. The beginning is the start of relations (Hilchot Issurei Biah 1:10), and for the matter of acquisition of marriage this suffices (compare above 3:5).
provided she is fit for relations. The chuppah acquires for marriage only if the woman is permitted for relations at that time.
but if she was a niddah. She is impure, and forbidden to her husband.
she is still like a betrothed woman. Until he is alone with her when she is fit for relations (below halakhah 6; and for the betrothal of a niddah see above 4:12).
who created everything for His glory. For all creation is for the glory of God.
Creator of man. For the very creation of man.
in His image, in the image of the likeness of His form. That man was created in the image of God (Genesis 1:27, 9:6).
and prepared for him from himself an everlasting structure. He formed the woman from man himself (see ibid. 2:21-22), so that together they could multiply, and humankind would endure forever.
may the barren one rejoice and be glad. She is the congregation of Israel, Zion.
in the gathering of her children into her midst in joy. In the redemption of Israel (see Isaiah 54:1-3).
loving companions. The groom and bride.
as You gladdened Your creation of old in the Garden of Eden. As You made Adam, the first man, glad when he was in the Garden of Eden.
let there be heard in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem. There they will celebrate, and the sound will be heard from afar.
the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the groom and the voice of the bride, etc. The prophecy about the good expected for the future of the Land of Israel (Jeremiah 33:10-11).
and he arranges all of them over the cup. He says the blessings in order, holding the cup.
and it turns out he says seven blessings. These six blessings and the blessing over wine.
with ten. In order to publicize the matter.
and free people. Who are not slaves.
and the groom is part of the number. He is included in the count of ten.
he does not repeat the blessings. Even though in the meantime she is still betrothed (see above halakhah 2).
ketubah. A document of financial obligation that the husband writes to his wife at the time of marriage, which she collects if he divorces her or she is widowed.
so that it not be easy in his eyes to send her away. They imposed a monetary obligation so that a person would not hurry to divorce his wife.
which was seven parts copper and one part silver. That was made of mixed metals in this proportion.
until a sela contains half a zuz of silver. A sela is four zuz, so its eighth is half a zuz.
barleycorns. Silver by volume of barleycorns.
at the beginning of Eruvin. 1:12.
and the denar is what is called a zuz everywhere, etc. Denar and zuz are the same, and the same names are used whether the coin is of pure silver or a coin of which an eighth is silver.
his relations are relations of harlotry. Like relations without marriage, because the woman does not rely on it in her mind and does not consent to marriage without a ketubah.
and they acquired from him. He established the force of his obligation by an act of kinyan (see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 11:1).
movable property against her ketubah. Objects worth the amount of the ketubah.
who waived her ketubah to her husband. She gave up the ketubah money to him.
who sold him her ketubah. So that he would not have to pay if he divorces her or dies.
the principal ketubah. The principal of the ketubah, which is a hundred or two hundred denarii (above halakhah 7).

one who sells her ketubah for the benefit of the claim. Who sold to another the right to collect her ketubah money if her husband divorces her or she is widowed. And since the woman might die first and the ketubah never come to be collected, he buys it for less than the amount written in it.
and if he divorces her he pays the ketubah to the buyer. If the husband divorces the woman, he pays the ketubah money to the one who bought it.
from free property. Property of the husband that is in his possession, and not from property he had at the time of writing and sold to others.
one who betroths his daughter and wrote her a ketubah. The father received betrothal for his daughter, and the betrothed wrote the betrothed woman a ketubah.
as we have explained. Above 3:11.
a widower. A man whose wife died.
he may. He is permitted (and see below 14:3).
it is permitted to betroth on any weekday. Even on the intermediate days of a festival (Hilchot Yom Tov 7:16). On a festival and on Shabbat it is forbidden (ibid. 1:17, Hilchot Shabbat 23:14).
even on the Ninth of Av. On which rejoicing is forbidden.
but they do not marry women on Friday or on Sunday. For the Sages enacted that the rejoicing of a wedding not be held on Friday or Sunday, out of concern for desecrating Shabbat.

and even on the intermediate days of a festival they do not marry women, as we have explained. Hilchot Yom Tov 7:16. But a man may take back his divorcee on the intermediate days of a festival (ibid.).
a virgin is married on Wednesday. And not on Sunday, so that he can labor over the feast for three days.
the claim of virginity. The husband's claim that his wife was not a virgin when he married her (below 11:9-17).
and it is not proper to do so. For it is proper to wait until she grows up (and see further above 3:19).
to provide for herself. To prepare clothing and jewelry for the wedding.
twelve months from the day of majority. From the day she became an adult, from which time she began preparing for her wedding.

so we give the man time to provide for himself. To prepare the needs of the feast and get ready for the wedding, and no sanctions are applied against him until the time arrives (as below halakhah 19).
if twelve months. In marrying a virgin.
and if thirty days. In marrying a non-virgin.
he becomes obligated for her food. He must give her food as if she were already married to him (see below 12:1).
because he cannot marry. As above halakhah 14.
a chalutzah. A yevamah for whom the yavam performed chalitzah (for the law of chalitzah see Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 1:1-2).
she is like a non-virgin. Even if she had no relations (see below halakhah 2).
a freed maidservant. A Canaanite maidservant who was freed, and her law is that of a convert (Hilchot Issurei Biah 12:17).
under three years and a day. Whose virginity returns after a time (below halakhah 3).

and the presumption is that a married woman has had relations... and they are like non-virgins in every respect. The assumption is that these women had relations, and therefore the Sages enacted their ketubah as for non-virgins even if they did not actually have relations (for further examples see Hilchot Issurei Biah 19:3 regarding a married woman, Hilchot Naarah Betulah 1:10 regarding a maidservant, a gentile and a captive).
injured by wood. Whose virginity was lost through an injury and not through relations (below halakhah 10).
on condition that she is a complete virgin. He did not know she was injured by wood.
and she was found injured by wood, her ketubah is a hundred. She does not lose her entire ketubah money, unlike when she is found to have had relations (below halakhah 16).
in the end she will return to being a virgin. The hymen will heal.
for the relations of a boy of nine years and a day are relations. Only from this age is the act defined as relations (Hilchot Issurei Biah 1:13).
blind. A blind woman.
who has marriage by their enactment. As explained above 4:9.
food. The husband's obligation to feed his wife (the details of the obligation are explained below 12:10 ff.).
from the terms of the ketubah. The obligations mentioned in the ketubah (detailed below 12:2).
he married her while deaf and she regained her hearing. He married her when she was deaf, and after a while she recovered from her deafness. And her ketubah is a hundred. For now she is a non-virgin.
because he wished to damage his property. For he deliberately lost his money, although he was not obligated to.
and became sane. Became of sound mind.
their wives have no claim at all against them. They cannot claim a ketubah, since at the time of marriage the husband was not of sound mind so as to be obligated for a ketubah.
where the Sages' enactment does not stand. The marriage of an insane person will not last long, and therefore the Sages did not enact marriage for him (see Hilchot Gerushin 10:23).
and in the end it will come to a complete marriage. When he grows up.
so that they not treat her as ownerless. So that she not be treated as available for harlotry.
signs. Signs of maturity (explained above 2:10).
even a boy of nine years and a day. Whose relations are relations (above halakhah 3).

and he kept her after he grew up, she has the principal ketubah of a maneh. This is the obligation fixed in every marriage (see above 10:7), and not the addition. He is obligated to give her a maneh (a hundred denarii) only, since she is not a virgin at the time the betrothal takes effect by Torah law.
and likewise a convert who converted, he and his wife, her ketubah is a maneh. For at the time of their first marriage they were gentiles.
for he kept her on this basis. He continued living with her as his wife on the understanding that he would give her a ketubah, even if he did not write it for her.
a claim of virginity. A claim that the woman was not found to be a virgin, in which case she loses her principal ketubah (below halakhah 16).
that her ketubah is a maneh. For she is presumed a non-virgin (above halakhot 1-2).
and one who is alone... has no claim of virginity. For it is possible that he himself had relations with her.
blood that flows. Blood that comes out as a result of tearing the hymen.
the pressure he finds in her. At the time of penetration through the hymen. Tenth: And her ketubah returns to a maneh. As with one injured by wood (above halakhah 3).

to place a general ban. By enactment of the Geonim, a person can place a ban (curse), without naming a specific individual, on anyone who makes a false claim against him (Hilchot Sheluchin VeShutafin 3:11; for the laws of the ban see Hilchot Talmud Torah 7:4-5).
for the matter is not certain for him. Since his claim is out of doubt, he cannot make her swear but only place a ban (see below halakhah 16).
and my purchase is a mistaken purchase. For he married her thinking she was a virgin, and obligated himself to the ketubah by mistake.
after I betrothed you, you had relations willingly. For one who commits adultery under her husband loses her ketubah (below 24:17), unlike if she was raped (ibid. halakhah 19).
they examine her. To determine whether she is a virgin.

he again has relations before witnesses. They prepare a cloth before witnesses and he is alone with her in their presence, and afterward they check whether there is blood on that cloth (Maggid Mishneh).
what was the matter, that you said, etc. On what basis did you say she was not a virgin?
and they soften her. In the bathhouse.
this is a claim of virginity. His claim is accepted, and he is exempt from paying the principal ketubah.
I found an open opening. That he felt she was not a virgin.
you turned. You did not have relations in the usual way but with a tilt.
and even though blood came out, etc. For if the opening is found open, the flowing blood is not a sign that she was a virgin.
she has no claim of blood, and she has a claim of an open opening. A claim of blood cannot be made against her, since her blood already dried up, but a claim of the absence of pressure can be made.
the Sages are the ones who enacted the principal ketubah for a woman. As explained above 10:7.

for the presumption is that a person does not toil over a feast and ruin it. The assumption is that a person does not want to cause the disruption of his own wedding joy himself, nor have his labor over the feast be in vain, and therefore if he made a claim of virginity he surely has a solid basis for his claim.
if she was secluded. If she was alone with him.

to make her lose the principal ketubah. For the principal ketubah, two hundred zuz for a virgin, is by rabbinic enactment, and they enacted that the husband be believed as explained in the previous halakhah.
but the addition she has. For the addition is by virtue of the husband's voluntary obligation (above 10:7), and he cannot be rid of it without clear proof.

he may make her swear. He is entitled to demand that she swear, similar to a borrower who claims against the lender that he already paid his debt (Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 14:2-3, following Maggid Mishneh, and see Yad Peshutah, Bnei Ahuvah and Or Sameach).
by taking hold of an object. Holding a Torah scroll while swearing (Hilchot Shevuot 11:8).
like all who swear and collect. Like the oaths by rabbinic enactment in which the plaintiff swears and collects his debt, which are made by taking hold of an object (Hilchot Toen VeNitan 1:2-3).
and she may place a general ban. See above halakhah 10.
that he wished to keep her. He wished to continue being married to her.
as we have explained. Above 10:10.
the freed woman. A maidservant who was freed. Second: Her she'er is her food. That he must supply her food (the details of the obligation are explained below halakhah 10 ff.).
her clothing, as it sounds. To supply her clothes (explained below chapter 13).
her conjugal rights, to come to her in the way of all the earth. To have marital relations (based on Genesis 19:31; the extent of the obligation is explained below chapter 14).
a condition of the court. A condition that does not derive from the agreement of the parties but from an obligation set by the court (and see below halakhah 5).
the principal of the ketubah. Payment of two hundred denarii for a virgin and a hundred for a non-virgin (above 10:7).
to heal her if she falls ill, to redeem her if she is captured, and to bury her when she dies. See below 14:17-24.
and to be supported... all the time of her widowhood. Until she collects her ketubah or marries another (see below chapter 18).
and that her daughters be supported from him. See below 19:10-11.

and that her male children inherit her ketubah in addition to their share in the inheritance with their brothers. That besides the father's inheritance, which is divided equally among all the sons, the woman's sons inherit their mother's ketubah (see below 19:1-2).
the work of her hands. The labor she does (for details see below chapter 21).
her found property. A lost object she found (Hilchot Gezelah VaAvedah 17:13).
eats the fruits of all her property. Uses the profits that come from her property (see below 22:7).
and if she dies in his lifetime he inherits her. Explained below 22:1-4, Hilchot Nachalot 1:8.
in exchange for. In return for.
his inheritance of her ketubah. His inheritance of the property mentioned in the ketubah.
I will not be supported and I will not work. I will not take food from you, and I will not work for you.
lest they not suffice for her. Lest her work not suffice for her livelihood.

the food is counted among the terms of the ketubah. Although the obligation of food is from the Torah (as above halakhah 2), since the Sages enacted that food is in exchange for the work of her hands, it is considered among the terms of the ketubah.
for he stipulated against what is written in the Torah. And a person cannot stipulate conditions contrary to Torah law in areas that are not monetary obligations (as explained above 6:9-10).
and she wrote to him that she received from them so much, and she did not receive. In effect there is a waiver and forgiveness of part of the sum.
for anyone who reduces... it is relations of harlotry. Like relations without marriage (above 10:9).
for it says of it, as a statute of judgment. "To say that this statute will not change and a condition is of no effect for it" (Hilchot Nachalot 6:1).
they set. They allot.
a medium meal. An average meal.
who is neither sick nor a glutton. For a sick person eats little, and a glutton eats much.
for lighting the lamp. For light.
three meals for Shabbat. For one is obligated to eat three meals on Shabbat (Hilchot Shabbat 30:9).
every Shabbat. Every week.
everything according to his wealth. For the completion of this law see below 13:5.
to send away. To divorce her.
that his hand can reach. That he is able to pay.
that he eat with her from Friday night to Friday night. That they eat together every Friday night.
terumah. Which is eaten in purity and must be guarded from becoming impure (Hilchot Terumot 7:1, 12:1).
and they shame. They embarrass.
and they urge. They plead, they request.
