who is not estimated. Whom the court has not estimated as to whether he has money.

because of charity. For the court compels one who does not give charity as he ought to give (Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 7:10). And the charity is given to his children, who take precedence over others (ibid. halakhah 13).
the presumption is that a person does not leave his house empty. That he left food in the house sufficient for this period.
they go down to his property and sell for her food. They sell his property to provide her food.
and they do not account against her for the work of her hands. They do not deduct from the food allowance what she will earn from the work of her hands.
she did not stand in judgment. Rather she sold his property on her own initiative.

the announcement. Publicizing the sale, a procedure done by the court before selling property (for the details of the announcement see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 12:8). When selling for the woman's food, no announcement is needed because of the urgency of the matter (ibid. halakhah 11).
an oath. To swear in court that she did not sell more than was proper for her.
until her husband comes and claims. That he left her money for food, and then she must swear (as explained below chapters 21-22).

they roll onto it that she did not sell. When she comes to collect her ketubah after her husband's death she must swear (below 16:4), and they add to this oath an additional declaration that she sold from the husband's property only for the food she needed (for the law of rolling an oath see Hilchot Toen VeNitan 1:12).
that comes out from under her hand. That is found with her as evidence that she has a ketubah and the terms of the ketubah.
she took her ketubah. She received her ketubah money.
she waived her ketubah. She gave up the monetary obligations in her ketubah.
as will be explained. Below 17:19, 18:1.
in the case of one whose husband went away, since she has food from the Torah. While she is still married to the husband (as above halakhah 2).
because she eats by rabbinic enactment. And the degree of obligation is lower, and therefore they do not allot her anything without it being established that she is entitled to food.

and also she is supported from the property of heirs, and one always argues for the heir. The court makes an effort to argue on behalf of the heir any claim that may help him (see below 18:23; for further examples see Hilchot Sheluchin VeShutafin 7:1, Hilchot Toen VeNitan 8:3). And because a widow's food is given to her from the property of the deceased husband's heirs, her power over it is less, and she is given nothing unless she proves she is entitled to food.
take the work of your hands for your food. Take for yourself the profit of your handiwork to buy food (see above halakhah 4).

for if she had not wanted this matter and had not been reassured, etc. For had she not agreed to this condition she could have objected, and from the fact that she did not object it follows that she wants it.
she sold for herself. Land of the husband.

by taking hold of an object. She holds a Torah scroll while swearing. And the Sages enacted that one who takes food swears this way, whether before she took or after she took, like those who swear and collect (see below 18:20; Bnei Ahuvah).
she waited until he came. She waited for his return.

the heset oath. An oath by enactment of the Sages of the Talmud imposed on one who denies his fellow's entire claim, and it is without taking an object (Hilchot Shevuot 11:7, 11:13, Hilchot Toen VeNitan 1:3).
I sold for food. I sold for my food.

she swears a heset oath. For in the case where she sold movable property, they did not enact an oath by taking an object (as above halakhah 21), and she swears a heset oath like one who denies the entire claim (Bnei Ahuvah).
she pressed herself day and night and worked and ate. She toiled and worked beyond the usual way, and so supported herself from the work of her hands.
one who prohibits his wife by vow from benefiting from him. Who forbade his wife by a vow to benefit from his property.
until such-and-such a time. He set a certain time for the prohibition of benefit.
and released his vow. For a person has the possibility to release his vow (for the details of releasing a vow see Hilchot Nedarim 4:5, Hilchot Shevuot chapter 6).
and he confirmed her vow for her. He agreed to her vow (Hilchot Nedarim 13:3). For if the husband objects, he can annul his wife's vows (ibid. 12:1).
who vowed to be a nazirite. She vowed to be a nazirite.
that she remain under him. That she remain his wife.

he must divorce and give a ketubah, for he could have annulled it and he confirmed it for her by his own will. He cannot claim he is divorcing her because of her actions and be exempt from paying her ketubah, since he himself could have cancelled the vow.
from year to year. Every year.
from the coinage of those days. The coin that was in use at the time these amounts were enacted (see above 10:8).
six denarii and a quarter. In denarii of pure silver.
their worn-out items. The clothes she received in the rainy season and which wore out from use.
and the worn ones, which are the surplus of clothing. The old and worn clothes that remain after she received new clothes.
and a head covering. A covering for her head.
from festival to festival. At each of the three pilgrimage festivals, Pesach, Shavuot and Sukkot.
the money is not the main thing. The obligation is not set specifically by the amount of money mentioned above.
at the lowest. The cheapest.
and a dwelling. A residence.
and a mat. A soft mat.
a courtyard. A back yard used for various needs.
outside of it. Outside the house.
and her forehead. Her brow.
and eye-paint and rouge. Cosmetic materials.
anyone for whom he is obligated to provide food. Anyone whom he is obligated to feed (see above 12:14-15).
they sell for his food. As explained there, 12:16-17.
according to their law regarding a claim of food. As explained above 12:21-22.
one who prohibits his wife. One who forbids his wife by vow.
from adorning herself with any of the kinds. From using any of the kinds of cosmetics.
a week. One week (and see Hilchot Deot 4:16).
from time to time. Twenty-four hours.
and a sieve. A strainer.
for it gives her a bad name among her neighbors. It causes her neighbors to speak ill of her, because she does not lend to them.
a miser. A stingy person.

places where it is the custom that a woman does not go out in the market, etc. In a place where women, when going out in public, were accustomed not to be satisfied with a cap on the head, but also wear a sheet of cloth covering the head and most of the body (and see below 24:12).
the cheap. The inexpensive.
now outside, now in the streets. This is how Scripture describes the promiscuous woman.
and the husband may. He is permitted.
one festival. Until one of the three pilgrimage festivals (Pesach, Shavuot, Sukkot) arrives, for it is the daughter's way to come to her father on the festivals.
people who are licentious. Who act licentiously toward women.
and they are established there. It is known that such people are there.
we listen to him. To establish the home in another place.
even though they were not established as licentious. Because living permanently beside them is highly harmful (compare above halakhah 13).
provinces. Cities.
there were three lands. For their borders see Hilchot Shemitah 7:9.
from a good dwelling to a bad dwelling. From a better settled place to a place less well settled than it.
to attend to herself and check herself well in the good dwelling. For in a better place people pay more attention to one another, and one living there must be more careful with dress and other needs.
light. Contemptible.
for all go up. Both the man and the woman (and the same applies to a slave and master, see Hilchot Avadim 8:9).
the conjugal rights mentioned in the Torah. The obligation to have marital relations, as explained above 12:2.
who have no work that weakens their strength. Whose work does not weaken them, unlike the other workers mentioned below.
twice every week. Twice a week.
once in the week. Once a week.
the donkey drivers. Donkey drivers who go from city to city.
the camel drivers. Camel drivers, who customarily travel long distances.
the sailors. Seamen, who customarily sail the sea for a long time.
their strength. Weakens them.
from Friday night to Friday night. Because of the commandment of enjoying Shabbat (Hilchot Shabbat 30:14).
a woman may prevent her husband. She is permitted to prevent him.
to go out from work... to work. To change occupations.
she'er, clothing and conjugal rights. The fixed obligations of every man to his wife (as explained above 12:2).
and he cannot compel them to live in one courtyard. As explained above 13:14.
according to number. For the obligation of conjugal rights is according to the husband's occupation, and is divided among his wives.
a laborer. One obligated to conjugal rights twice a week (above halakhah 1).
once a month. According to the conjugal time of Torah scholars, which is once a week (above halakhah 1).
one who prohibits his wife. One who forbids his wife by vow.
words of disgrace. Embarrassing speech.
turns herself during relations, etc. So that the seed not be absorbed in her body.
let him annul his vow. Let him release his vow.

because he is obligated to her. And therefore if he forbade her, the vow does not take effect, since he cannot forbid himself something he owes her (Hilchot Nedarim 12:9). And if he swore, he transgresses the prohibition of a vain oath, like one who swears to cancel a commandment, and the oath is void (Hilchot Shevuot 1:6-7, 5:14-15).

the pleasure of your intimacy is forbidden to me. He forbade himself the pleasure of marital relations with her, so that the vow does not relate to his obligation toward her but to his own pleasure (Hilchot Nedarim 1:30).
for we do not feed a person something forbidden to him. We do not compel him to have relations with her because his vow took effect, despite his obligation to her.
for you have no conjugal rights greater than this one. This is the conjugal time of sailors (above halakhah 1).
let him take permission from her. To continue living with her without marital relations.
to send away at once. To divorce her immediately.
without any ketubah at all. Because she caused the divorce and not the husband.
and she takes her worn items that remain. She takes with her the used property that was hers originally.
that she brought in to her husband. That she brought with her from her father's house.

and he became liable for their responsibility. The husband obligated himself in the ketubah document to pay her their value as it was when he received them, even if they were lost or the value of the property fell, and these are "iron sheep property" (see below 16:1).
from property for which he did not become liable. And these are "usufruct property" (see there).
that he bought for her. That the husband bought for her.
weeks. Weeks.
they consult her. They find out from her the reason for her rebellion, to persuade her to retract.
and they do not give her a get until twelve months. Lest she retract.
whose time to marry has come. As explained above 10:17.
and likewise a yevamah who did not want to be taken in yibbum. For more see Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 2:10.
this rebellious woman. Who wishes to cause her husband distress (as opposed to the one who said she was repelled by her husband, mentioned above in halakhah 8).
property she brought in to him. Property she brought from her father's house and for which the husband assumed responsibility (see there).
and their worn items remain. And what wore out of them remains.
if she seized, etc. But usufruct property, even if the husband seized it, is taken out of his hand since it is the wife's property.
they do not take out of his hand. Whereas for one who says "I am repelled by him," the husband has no ownership of the property she brought from her father's house (there).
as long as she wants to stay. As long as she still wants the marriage.
he shall not diminish. And the beginning of the verse: "her she'er, her clothing and her conjugal rights."
for if he hates, let him send away. If a man hates his wife, he must divorce her (for more see Hilchot Gerushin 10:21).
to afflict. To withhold marital relations.
because there is no act in it. For he refrained from doing, and one does not receive lashes for a transgression unless there is an act involved (see Hilchot Yerushalmi Sanhedrin 18:1-2).
in the way of all the earth. Having marital relations.
they place a ban. They impose a ban (see above 11:10).
they ask the one claimed against. They ask the one against whom the claim is made to reach a compromise.
he must heal her. The husband must pay her medical expenses (and this is one of the terms of the ketubah; see above 12:2).

and said to her, behold your ketubah is set aside, etc. That he gives her the amount of her ketubah and puts before her the choice: either to be healed with this sum and remain married to him, or that he divorce her, and in any case he is obligated to pay her only her ketubah.
the way of the land. The custom of decent people.
if she was captured he must redeem her. If the woman was taken captive, the husband must pay her ransom (and this too is one of the terms of the ketubah; see above 12:2).

if he was a priest, she is already forbidden to him. For a captive woman is forbidden to a priest, lest she was raped during captivity (Hilchot Issurei Biah 18:17; and see further ibid. halakhot 6-8).
to her city. To her own town.
for more than her value. To pay more than her worth.
like the other captive women. Who are redeemed according to their value and not more (see Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 8:12).
even if her price was up to ten times her ketubah. Even if the price was ten times the amount of the ketubah.
he has only enough for her redemption. For the ransom sum is all the money he has.
and he is overseas. He is abroad and is not here to redeem her.
they go down to his property and sell with an announcement. See above 12:16.
a vow for which he is obligated to divorce her. As detailed above 12:23-24, 13:8-10, ibid. 12-13, 14:5-6, and below 21:3.
from prohibitions of negative commandments. These prohibitions are detailed above 1:7.
and he redeems her. As explained above halakhah 18.
eulogy and dirges according to the custom of the whole country. Words of honor and mourning songs as customary in that place.
flutes. Which were customarily played at funerals.

she goes up with her husband and does not go down. The husband's obligations to his wife are set according to his status when his status is higher than hers, and according to her status when her status is higher than his (for clothing and dwelling see below 18:3).
they take from her husband against his will. The burial expenses.
and sell without an announcement. They sell the property without a public announcement, because of the urgency of the matter (Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 12:11).
and according to his honor or according to her honor. As above halakhah 23.
that she permitted. She gave permission.

that he already fulfilled the commandment of being fruitful and multiplying. As will be explained below from halakhah 4 on. Third: And was lost in it. He occupied himself with her, based on the verse "be ever intoxicated with her love" (Proverbs 5:19).
like Ben Azzai. A sage of the Tannaitic era, who did not marry because of his devotion to Torah.
and even if he had children. And already fulfilled the commandment of being fruitful and multiplying.
a sinful thought. A thought of transgression.
male and female. And "the commandment is male and female, in which is the continuation of the species" (Commentary on the Mishnah, Yevamot 6:7).

a saris... an aylonit. Who cannot beget. Fifth: Children's children are like children. Grandchildren are considered children for the purpose of fulfilling the commandment of being fruitful and multiplying.
in his gentile state. While he was a gentile.
and he converted, he and they, he has fulfilled this commandment. Even though by law they are not considered relatives (Hilchot Issurei Biah 14:11).
a slave who was freed. Who is also considered like a convert.
he has no lineage. The relationship between the slave and his descendants has no significance.
ten years. Like Abraham our father, who after ten years in which Sarah bore him no child took Hagar (Yevamot 64a).
who did not recognize her. Who did not know she was an aylonit from the outset.
as will be explained. Below 24:2-3.
shoots semen like an arrow. That the seed is expelled from him with force.
principal and addition. As explained above 10:7.
as we have said. In the previous halakhah.
leave the money in the presumption of its owners. Since the money is presumed to be the husband's, he is not obligated to pay in cases of doubt.
we listen to her. We accept her claim for divorce.
she needs children for her old age. To help her.
for he did not write her the addition on condition that she leave of her own will and take it. But on condition that he live with her (see below 24:3).
within ten years. During those ten years.
and perhaps he was not worthy of being built up through her. It may not depend on her, but the combination of the two is not suited for being fruitful and multiplying.
so that he will stay with her. An additional time, since the ten years are counted from the day she miscarried.
for by this claim he would become obligated to pay her ketubah. Now; and because he claims he is not obligated to pay now, he makes her swear.
she is permitted to marry a second. Perhaps the reason she did not bear to the first husband was because of him and not because of her.
she shall not marry a third. Because she is established as barren.
unless he has another wife, etc. In which case she is permitted to marry him at the outset (above halakhah 7).
who came to court. And did not stay with her husband ten years.
does not shoot like an arrow. The seed is not expelled with force.
and they roll with her. They try to persuade her.
to stay. To remain with her husband.
the law of a rebellious wife. See above 14:8-14.
that she not be suspected. Of adultery or the like.
to warn his wife. To warn her to conduct herself in modesty (for more see Hilchot Sotah 4:18-19).
only with her consent. Willingly (for more see Hilchot Deot 5:4).
and she shall not demand marital relations with her mouth. She shall not request explicitly.
in the matter. In the subject.
obedient. To marital relations.
from ugliness and from what resembles ugliness. Acts of immodesty (below 24:15).
honors his wife more than himself. With clothing and jewelry (and see Hilchot Deot 5:10).
excessively. Much. Walking in the desire of his heart. Doing his will.
that a woman brings in to her husband. That she brings with her when she marries him, so that it be shared by both of them and they use it.

although they are written in the ketubah document, they are not called ketubah. Although these assets are detailed in the ketubah document, the laws of the ketubah do not apply to them, but they have a separate definition and law.

and if the husband accepted responsibility, etc. One kind of property given as dowry is property for which the husband accepts responsibility, and in the case of divorce or widowhood he must return to the woman its value as it was when it was given, no less and no more.
iron sheep property (nichsei tzon barzel). So called because their value is preserved, just as iron does not wear away.

and if he did not accept responsibility for the dowry... it is called usufruct property (nichsei melog). The second kind of property given as dowry is property for whose value the husband did not accept responsibility, and he must return it in the condition it is in now, after the divorce or widowhood, even if it has declined or risen from its original value at the time the dowry was given.
the addition. The sum the husband adds to the principal ketubah (above 10:7).
we have already informed that the Sages enacted a ketubah for the woman, etc. Above 10:7.
from the worst of his property. Unlike another creditor, who collects his debt from the middling quality of the debtor's land (Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 19:1).
that when she comes to collect. The principal ketubah and the addition (for the law of collecting the dowry see below 18:9).
she may not collect until she swears. As with one who collects from the property of heirs, who must swear (Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 14:1).
holding an object. Holding a Torah scroll, as in the law of those who swear and collect (see above 11:16).
that he did not leave with her anything. That the husband did not leave in her hands property from which to collect her ketubah.
and that she did not sell him her ketubah. For a woman may sell it, either to her husband or to others (below 17:17; and see above 10:10).
she waived it. She relinquished to her husband her right to the ketubah (see below 17:19).
and they appraise for her everything she is wearing. They assess the value of the clothes she is wearing, which came from her husband's property.
for he bought them for her and she acquired them. He bought them on her behalf, and she received them and they became her own.
and he wants to divorce her, not she him. Since he is divorcing her on his own initiative, he has waived the value of her clothes.
that a widow may collect her ketubah only from land. Just as the movable property of orphans is not subject to a lien in favor of a creditor (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 8:11).
from the improvement in the value of the property. What was added to the value of the property.
the daughters are to be supported. They receive maintenance from their father's estate (above 12:2, below 19:10).
and she does not seize etc.. If the husband sold his land, the woman may collect ("seize") her ketubah from the buyer out of the land, minus the amount of the improvement.
for a creditor collects the improvement. See Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 21:1.
and these are among the leniencies of the ketubah. The limits on collecting improvements are among the matters in which the law of the ketubah is more lenient than the laws of other promissory notes.
the lesser of the coins. The coin of lower value.
plain money. Without specifying exactly.
a specific coin. A particular coin.
as will be explained in Hilchot Loans. Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 4:11.
the Geonim in all the yeshivot. The heads of the yeshivot after the Talmud was sealed.
even from movable property. Because reality changed, and much stable wealth is no longer in land but in movables.
in the way they enacted for a creditor to collect from movables. See, for example, Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 11:11.
and it spread. It became widespread and accepted.
the other conditions of the ketubah. See above 12:2.

from the ketubah of male children. The husband's undertaking that the sons will collect their mother's ketubah after her death, in addition to their share of the inheritance (above 12:2; and see further below 19:1-9).
that they write in the ketubah: both from real estate and from movables. That the ketubah document state explicitly that collection may be made both from land and from movables.
for this is a monetary condition. For if the matters were written explicitly and agreed upon, they are binding, since every monetary condition stands (Hilchot Mechirah 13:3, Hilchot Sechirut 2:9).
by the enactment of the later authorities. The enactment of the Geonim.
if he knew of this enactment of the Geonim, she collects. If he knew that the ketubah is collected from movables too, he married her on that understanding.
they deliberate much on this matter. They examine the circumstances of the case carefully (Yad Peshutah).

for the enactment of the Geonim has no force etc.. The conditions of the ketubah are an enactment of the Sanhedrin, and therefore bind even if not written explicitly (above 12:5). But the enactment of the Geonim does not have such force, and if the husband did not agree in advance that collection be made from movable property, money cannot be taken from the heirs on the basis of the enactment (for another example see Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 11:11).
guarantors and sureties for her ketubah. Bound for its payment.
to seize them. To collect them from the buyers.
unencumbered property. Property that was not sold.
by oath. For the text of the oath see above 5:4.
like the law of all creditors. That they swear to the buyer who holds the encumbered property (see Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 14:1, 22:10).
and this enactment. That all his property be encumbered.
so that her ketubah not be light in his eyes. That the ketubah debt be as serious as other debts, "so that it not be light in his eyes to divorce her" (above 10:7).
she is made to swear only outside the court. In such a way that she swears loudly enough for the oath to be heard by the judges in the court (see Responsa of the Rambam 420).
lest she not be careful about herself in the oath. Lest she swear even though she received some payment, and they did not want her to stumble in an oath, which is extremely grave.
to bind her by a vow. That something be forbidden to her by a vow if she is lying.

and they bind her by a vow in court. So that if she received any payment, the thing by which she was bound becomes forbidden to her. As for a vow, they did not suspect she would lie, since the fear of vows is greater for them than the fear of oaths (Yerushalmi Gittin 4:3).
for she has no ketubah until she swears. And they cannot swear, since a person does not bequeath an oath to his children (Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 17:3).
lest the husband annul. The present husband. For a husband can annul his wife's vows (Hilchot Nedarim 12:1).
he designated land for her in her ketubah. From which she is to collect her ketubah.
the boundaries. The borders of the field.
without an oath. Since he designated land for her, there is no concern that he left other property in her hands.
she who impairs her ketubah etc.. The following halachot (through halachah 20) do not deal with the oath enacted for a widow (above 5:4), but with cases in which even a divorcee must swear.
she collects only by oath. Like a creditor who impairs his note (Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 14:1).
even if she was precise in the accounting etc.. That she calculated the husband's payments exactly, down to half a perutah.
she collects her entire ketubah only by oath. Like a creditor when one witness testifies that his note has been paid (Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 14:1).
one who collects not in his presence. She receives payment of the ketubah in the husband's absence.
she collects only by oath. Like a creditor (Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 14:1; and see there 13:1-2 for the conditions of collection).
an amanah. An oral agreement that the amount written will not be collected in full.
they say to her: swear and take. As with a creditor (Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 14:2).
he stipulated with her. When he married her.
if she comes to collect from his heirs she must swear. That he released her only from him.
from encumbered property. Property encumbered for payment of her ketubah that was sold to others.
comes out from under her hand. Is found with her.
they rely on the condition of the court. On the fact that they enacted a ketubah for the woman, and therefore do not bother to write it.
and for how long. Until when.
for if she had not waived, she would not have remained silent all this time. From the fact that she did not claim it throughout the years, it is evident that she waived her ketubah.

and she is not with the heirs etc.. For if she lives in the husband's house with the heirs, she can claim that she did not demand it because she was embarrassed before them, not because she waived it.

she may make him swear the Torah oath, since he admitted to part of the claim. Since the husband admitted that he owes one hundred of the two hundred claimed, she can obligate him to the oath that the Torah requires of one who partially admits a claim (see Hilchot To'en ve-Nit'an 1:1).

and a minor is believed to testify when he grows up. He was a minor when he saw the event and is now an adult. We rely on this testimony because most women marry as virgins, and also because the ketubah is a rabbinic enactment (Hilchot Edut 14:3).
as we have said. Above, halachah 22.
she is believed. And she may marry another on the basis of this presumption (Hilchot Gerushin 12:4, above 4:13).
brazen. Insolent.

he does not give the addition. We rely on the presumption only with regard to the principal of the ketubah, because the principal rests on a rabbinic enactment, and if she is permitted to marry another, he is necessarily bound by this enactment. But the addition is treated as an ordinary obligation between one person and another, and he is not required to pay without clear proof (Yad Peshutah; and see Lechem Mishneh).
a receipt. A document proving payment of the debt.
and he makes her swear holding an object. As with a husband who told his wife to swear (above, halachah 19).
and he swears a heset oath. For he denies her entire claim regarding the addition.
as we have explained. Above, halachot 21-22.
she produced two bills of divorce and two ketubot. Against one man, whom she married twice and was divorced from twice, and each time he wrote her a new ketubah.
if both are equal. In amount.

the later one cancelled the earlier. Since the only difference between them is the date of the ketubah, we assume the later ketubah was written to cancel the earlier (as with other documents, see Hilchot Zechiyah u-Matanah 5:9).
and she seizes only from the date of the later one. She may collect from land the husband sold only from the time in the second document, not from the earlier time in the first.
she collects on whichever she wishes. The second did not cancel the first, but serves as a possible alternative (see there, halachah 8).
he took her back on her first ketubah. He married her the second time on the basis of the existing, unpaid ketubah, and did not write her a new one.
a bill of divorce and a ketubah after her husband's death. He married her a second time after divorcing her, and died afterwards, and she claims two ketubot.
if the bill of divorce precedes the ketubah. From the dates of the documents it can be known that he divorced her by a get, and took her back on the basis of a new ketubah.
if it is not their custom to write a ketubah. As above, halachah 28.
and if the ketubah preceded the bill of divorce etc.. It is understood that the ketubah is from their first marriage, and he took her back after the divorce on the basis of this ketubah.
in Hilchot Divorce. 12:15.
and they make her swear. As with a widow who comes to collect her ketubah from the heirs (above, halachah 4).
but only to take a ketubah during his lifetime. She wants to receive the ketubah while her husband is alive, and they do not give it to her.
and they do not give her a ketubah. Because it is uncertain whether she said so because she wants to marry or in order to collect her ketubah.
and if she seized. She herself took hold of property in order to collect the ketubah.

whichever one was married first takes her ketubah first. Because the lien on the property takes effect from the time the ketubah was written, priority in collecting is determined by the order in which they married (see Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 20:1-4).
and none of them takes except by oath. All of them must swear that they are taking lawfully from the estate, in the text of the oath explained above 16:4.
what the one before her left over. What remains of the husband's property after the one before her has collected.
if there was a promissory note against him. The husband owed money by a note to another person.
where the land... was acquired by him. It was already his before he married a wife and borrowed money, and it became encumbered for these debts at the time they were written in the document.
in a place where they write the hours. In a place where it was customary to note in the document the hour as well as the date.
for there is no one with priority there. None of the holders of the documents has priority over the others.
for there is no law of priority with movables. No one has preference regarding this property (and see below, halachah 6).
enough for the debt and the ketubah. In an amount sufficient to pay the debt and the ketubah.
the creditor takes the money. Because he himself lent money, and it is proper that he receive his money back.
and it had no law of priority. As in the cases explained above, halachot 2-3.
and if anything is left for the woman. A share from which to collect.
for the creditor has lost and spent his money. In the loan he gave the husband, and therefore it is proper to give him priority in collecting the debt.

and the woman lost nothing, for just as a man wants to take a wife, a woman wants to be married. Although agreeing to marriage involves some concession, the woman wants it even more, and from her perspective it is a gain, not a loss.
that the Geonim enacted. See above 16:7.
property of iron sheep. See above 16:1, and the commentary there.
like the other creditors. And they have no preference over her, since she lost some of her own (see above, halachah 4).
when the money is divided according to the number of wives. They divide the money equally according to the number of wives.
to the smallest of them. To the one whose ketubah is the smallest of all.
the remainder. What is left (see Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 20:4).
one who guarantees a woman's ketubah. One who undertakes to pay the woman her ketubah if the husband does not pay (see Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 25:2-3, and there, halachah 6).
that they made a kinyan from his hand. That his undertaking was given force by an act of acquisition.
for he did a mitzvah. For he helped the couple to marry.
and she lost nothing. The woman does not lose money (see above, halachah 4), and for these reasons the guarantor does not bind himself absolutely.
and he firmly resolves and transfers. He resolves in his mind to obligate himself to pay.
a surety for a ketubah. A guarantor who took upon himself to pay the ketubah even where the husband is able to pay (see Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 25:4-5).
one who divorces his wife. And another person was a guarantor for her ketubah.
he binds her by a vow of benefit. He vows that she may not benefit from him, so that she will not remarry him.

and it turns out they are scheming against the property of this one. A ruse to claim payment of the ketubah from another person, when they truly do not wish to divorce. 10. One who consecrates his property. To the Temple.

and afterwards she collects from the one who redeems from the hand of the Temple treasury. The Temple treasury sells the property to one who undertakes to redeem it and pay the woman her ketubah, since the lien for the debts of the one who consecrated returns to the property after redemption (see Hilchot Arachin va-Charamin 7:14-18).
but one who divorces his wife and she comes to seize from the buyers. In an ordinary case, where there were no guarantors or consecration, but people who bought the husband's property.
she swears and seizes. See above 16:10.
I have no claim or dispute with you. I will not collect from you the property you bought, even though it was encumbered to me.
I did a favor for my husband. She can say that she wrote it to appease her husband, and did not truly agree to give up her lien (for a similar claim see below 22:18).
they made a kinyan from the woman first. Since the woman bound herself by a kinyan before the husband sold the field, there is no concern that she did it to prevent a quarrel.
and it was invalidated. It was eventually cancelled.
for in the first case, when she did not want to, she did not go along with her husband's wish. From the first sale it was proven that she does not do things in order to appease her husband.
who had two wives. And he married them at different times.
and it was an effective kinyan. As explained in the previous halachah.
because she came first. For priority is determined by the order of marriage (above, halachah 1).
and they come back around. They return again and again to the same situation.
that they reach a compromise. That they come to an agreement among themselves (for a similar law see Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 19:8).
she swears. As explained above 16:4.
experts. People knowledgeable in the laws of the Torah.
in the valuation of the land. In assessing the value of the land.

and the guarantee of the sale is on the property of the orphans. The orphans' property, which is the rest of the deceased's estate, is encumbered to the buyer, and he may collect from it if the land he bought is taken from him by law (for example, if witnesses testify that it was stolen).
with a proclamation. Publicizing the sale (see above 12:16).
and in Hilchot Loans. Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 12:8.
and even though they are three etc.. Even so they are not considered a court, and do not need to sell by proclamation.
between herself and herself. Not in the presence of three.
at an equal value. At the true value of the land.
the widow's oath. See above 16:4.
she appraised it for herself. She collected the land for herself in payment of her ketubah.
and she has nothing. She receives no more.
and she sold land worth a hundred and a dinar for a hundred, her sale is void. Since she has no right to sell for more than the value of her ketubah.
to this one. To one buyer.
a woman may sell her ketubah. She may sell the right to collect the ketubah to others.
that one. The buyer or recipient of the gift.
or before she swore. That she does not receive her ketubah (above 16:12).
she pledged it. She gave it as security for a debt she undertook.
even many times. Until she collects the full amount.
she did not lose the other conditions of the ketubah. Which were detailed above 12:2.
an heir corresponding to this ketubah etc.. He inherits an amount equal to her ketubah, in addition to his share with his brothers in the inheritance of their father (explained below 19:1-9).
one who waives her ketubah etc.. When she waives her ketubah she gives up all her rights.
like other waivers, which do not require etc.. See Hilchot Zechiyah u-Matanah 3:4 (regarding witnesses); Hilchot Mechirah 5:11-13 (regarding a kinyan).

and it must not be words of jest and mockery or words of astonishment, but with sound mind. That the waiver was not made in jest or in astonishing statements that could not be meant, but with deliberate consideration.
a widow is supported from the property of the heirs. For her husband undertook to support her from his property after his death (above 12:2).
the potiki. Property designated for collecting the debt (see Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 18:3).
and a residence. A place to live.

she lives in the residence in which she lived during her husband's lifetime. The heirs have no authority to remove her from there to another residence, for one of the conditions of the ketubah is: "You shall dwell in my house" (Bavli Ketubot 103a).
the heirs are not required to build it. That same residence. Rather, they give her another residence befitting her dignity (below, halachah 3).
leave me and I will build it from my own means - they do not listen to her. Even if she wants to build it at her own expense they do not allow her, since she has no rights at all in the residence.
she may not strengthen its crack and may not plaster it. She may not repair the cracks or replaster the residence.
for the husband had a house only by rental. During her husband's lifetime they did not live in a house of his own, but rented a dwelling.
a residence according to her dignity. A place to live suitable for her, according to her status.
she rises with him and does not descend, even after death. His high status is taken into account even after his death (and see above 14:23).
the blessing of the household is greater. For the expense of food is proportionally smaller when there are more people in the household.
a kav. A measure of volume.
together. Jointly.
according to the blessing of the household. The proportional share of the joint maintenance.
because she is young and they are young etc.. If she claims that she is young and they are her age, and that if they live together a bad reputation might arise about them, her claim is accepted.
and the surplus of the widow's maintenance. Food that was provided to her and that she did not need.
for she has no fixed allowance. Her expenses were not determined in advance.
if she is taken captive, the heirs are not required to redeem her. If she was taken captive, the heirs are exempt from paying her ransom, since the duty of redemption is on the husband alone.

even if she was a yevamah. In which case it is a mitzvah for the deceased's brother to marry his widow (Hilchot Yibbum va-Chalitzah 1:1), and even so the bond of yibbum does not obligate redeeming her. 6. The widow's oath. That a widow must swear before collecting her ketubah (see above 16:4).
and they are obligated for her burial. For burial is in place of the ketubah (see above 12:4).
the widow's handiwork. The work she does.
take the handiwork of your hands for your maintenance. Take for yourself the profit of your handiwork to buy your food (compare above 12:4). 7. Work that a wife does for her husband. Below 21:1-7.
except for mixing the cup etc.. Tasks that show intimacy with the husband (below 21:8, Hilchot Issurei Biah 11:9), which does not apply toward the heirs.
and the produce of the property. The profits that came from her property.
and the heir has nothing in them. For the Sages gave them to the husband alone.
her nedunya. The property she brought with her from her father's house (see above 16:1-2).
without an oath. Unlike the ketubah itself (compare above 16:4).
they increased in his husband's lifetime. The value of the property rose.
for the surplus belongs to the husband. And therefore his heirs acquire it after his death.
her heirs inherit her nedunya. Unlike the ketubah itself (compare there, halachah 12).

who seized movables in order to be supported from them. She took hold of movables from her husband's property. Had she not taken them, she could collect maintenance from the heirs only from land (above 16:5).
a talent of gold. A talent is a large unit of weight for weighing metals, and a talent of gold is an enormous sum.
they do not take it out of her hand. Since she has a right to maintenance, they leave what she seized in her possession, although she could not take movables from the heirs (see Tosafot Ketubot 96a).
and they fix. They allot.
and they account with her. For the total of her handiwork that she will do, and deduct it from the maintenance.
until she has no maintenance. Until she is no longer entitled to maintenance, for example when she claims her ketubah or becomes betrothed (above, halachah 1).

and likewise if she seized movables for her ketubah etc.. For the law of the ketubah is like that of any promissory note: movables are not encumbered for its payment after the debtor's death, only land. But if the creditor preceded and seized movables during the debtor's lifetime, he may collect from them after his death (Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 11:7-8).

that the Geonim enacted etc.. Above 16:7. 12. And she cannot prevent them. That she collects from the movables, but their substance is not encumbered for the debt. Even if he stipulated about it explicitly. The husband took it upon himself when writing the ketubah (see above 16:8). And in this. In this way.
but if he left land. From which she collects by virtue of the Sages' enactment (above 16:5).
and the daughters are supported. From the father's property after his death, which is one of the conditions of the ketubah (above 12:2; below 19:10-16).

who fell before a yavam. Her husband died without children, and she must marry her husband's brother (the yavam), or perform chalitzah for him in order to marry another (Hilchot Yibbum va-Chalitzah 1:1-2).

in the first three months. In which she is forbidden to enter yibbum or perform chalitzah, lest she be pregnant by her deceased husband (Hilchot Gerushin 11:18; Hilchot Yibbum va-Chalitzah 1:19). And because she is held back on his account, she is supported from his property.
and if the pregnancy was recognized, and likewise if he left her pregnant. She must wait until she gives birth, and if the child is viable she is exempt from yibbum (Hilchot Yibbum va-Chalitzah 1:5).
the pregnancy was recognized. It is evident that she is pregnant, usually after three months.
neither from the husband's nor from the yavam's. She is not held back on account of the husband, and the yavam has not yet become obligated for her maintenance.
and he stood in judgment. The court ruled that he must perform yibbum or chalitzah.
without any oath at all. Unlike an ordinary widow, for it is clear that she received no payment from him (compare below, halachot 19-20).
a minor. Who cannot perform chalitzah until he grows up, and his yibbum also has no complete validity (Hilchot Yibbum va-Chalitzah 1:16).

let such-and-such a place be for maintenance, he has increased her maintenance. For the meaning of this wording is that a particular piece of land is designated for maintenance, but it does not imply that it alone is to be it.
and if it was its rent. The profit from that land.
for maintenance... that place only. Which implies that this land alone is to serve for her support.
he fixed. He set a measure.

regarding a woman whose husband went overseas. And she claimed her maintenance. The law is that she swears only if her husband returns from overseas and claims that she sold improperly (see above 12:16).
and anyone who collects from the property of orphans etc.. As explained in Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 14:1.
they make her swear at the outset. That he did not leave her money for her maintenance (as above 16:4).

and they sell without proclamation. Without the need to publicize, because of the urgency of the matter (see above 12:16, Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 12:11). At an equal value. At the true value of the land (for a similar law see above 17:14).
thirty days' food, thirty days' food. He gives her each time money sufficient for thirty days' food.
they do not account with her for her handiwork. They do not deduct from the maintenance the amount of her future handiwork (compare above 12:16).
they take it. For the widow's handiwork belongs to the heirs (above, halachah 6).
for if the heirs were minors, the court accounts with her etc.. For the court must protect the rights of the orphans (Hilchot Nachalot 10:5).
for the ketubah document does not come out from under her hand etc.. It is not in her possession (and see above 17:17-18).
we argue for him. The court argues on behalf of the heir any argument that could help him (see above 12:18, and there is a dispute on this law).
and she said: my husband died. She is believed so that she may marry (see above 16:31).
she said: my husband divorced me - she is not believed. To marry. Since it is known that she was a married woman, this assumption cannot be annulled by her statement alone (Hilchot Gerushin 12:1).
and she is supported from his property up to the amount of her ketubah in any case. From any perspective, she is entitled to such an amount.
she has maintenance. Since because of him she cannot marry another man (Rashi Ketubot 97b).
as long as she has not married. For the property is still encumbered for her maintenance.

she swears a heset oath. An oath enacted by the Sages, imposed on one who denies the entire claim against him. Here the property is in her possession, and the orphans seek to take it from her (Maggid Mishneh).
and once she has married. When she has no maintenance (see above, halachah 1), and the property is in the possession of the orphans, and she wants to take it from them.
she has no maintenance. As above, halachah 1.
this is like one who claimed part of the principal and left part of it. And she has maintenance, like one who sold part of the ketubah (there).
plain. She did not specify what she meant.

that his male children inherit their mother's ketubah and her nedunya. This condition is called "the ketubah of male children." It was enacted so that a man would be generous in giving property to his married daughter, knowing that this property would remain with his grandchildren, her children, even if she died before her husband and he inherited her, and her husband's other heirs would not take it from them (Bavli Ketubot 52b).

and her nedunya that she brought in as property of iron sheep. Even this sum of the debt is written in the ketubah (see above 16:1). 2. And she died in his lifetime. And the husband inherited the woman's property.
and he left two thousand. This is the total of the inheritance the husband left.
it turns out that in the hand of the first wife's son etc.. After they divided equally among themselves the remaining eight hundred dinars.
where he left more than the amount of the two ketubot by one dinar or more. The entire estate is larger than the amount of the two ketubot by one dinar or more.

it turns out this condition cancels the equal division of inheritance among sons, which is from the Torah. An equal division would not take place in a significant amount (a dinar), and the Sages did not enact the law of the ketubah of male children where it would cancel the Torah's law.

more than all the ketubot by a dinar. Besides all the ketubah sums, there is an additional dinar in the estate. The dinar is a fixed sum, regardless of the question of how many it is to be divided among.
they raise. We accept their value at a greater amount than their market price.
they appraise. They assess.
that increased or decreased after their father's death. Their value rose or fell.
that has a promissory note against it equal to the surplus. He owes others money in the amount of the whole surplus of the ketubot.

it does not reduce etc.. The debt does not reduce the inheritance, since it is considered that they inherited that surplus, and thus the Torah's inheritance is fulfilled, even though they will pay it afterwards to the creditor.
the widow's oath. Which she must take when she comes to collect her ketubah (see above 16:4), and since she swore, her heirs inherit her ketubah from her.

for they do not inherit their mother's ketubah by this condition. For here their inheritance is not by virtue of the enactment that male children inherit their mother's ketubah, but by Torah law, that sons inherit their mother when she has no husband.

and afterwards the sons of the first wife inherit. Even if no property remained beyond the ketubah. Because the widow's ketubah is like a debt, which is considered an inheritance and does not reduce the surplus (above, halachah 6).

and if she died before she swore etc.. The second wife's sons do not inherit her right to the ketubah, for they cannot swear in her place (see above 16:12), nor as the ketubah of male children, for she did not die in his lifetime.
and the heirs of the first wife precede the heirs of the second. According to the order of marriage, just as the first wife precedes the second if they were collecting themselves (above 17:1).
he does not seize from encumbered property. From the father's property that was sold to others.
like all heirs. For this is not a debt collected even from encumbered property (Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 18:1), but an inheritance.

her handiwork and her finds are hers, not the brothers'. Unlike a supported widow, whose handiwork belongs to the heirs (above 18:6), because a man wants his daughter to have ample means (Bavli Ketubot 43a).
they fix. They set an amount.
in the way they fix for a widow. Above 18:2.
without proclamation, as they sell for the widow's food and clothing. See there, halachah 20.
for a woman they fix according to her dignity and her husband's dignity. There, halachah 3. As he treated her in his lifetime (see above 13:5).
and for daughters they fix only what suffices for them. As he was obligated to provide for his minor children during his lifetime (there, halachah 6).
and daughters do not swear. Although a widow who claims maintenance swears (above 18:19).
comes out from under their hand. Is found in their possession as proof of the ketubah's validity.
lest their mother waived her ketubah. That she relinquished the husband's obligations to her, the ketubah and its conditions (above 17:19; for a similar law see above 18:23).
they do not listen to him. They do not do what he commanded, because he is bound by these conditions from the time of the marriage.
and the gift of one who is deathly ill. Which he gave when he was dangerously ill and about to die.
as will be explained. Hilchot Zechiyah u-Matanah 8:8.

the gift and the obligation of the property under these conditions come as one etc.. And therefore the gift is postponed until they collect what is due to them under the conditions of the ketubah. But if he sold his property in his lifetime or gave it as a healthy person's gift, they are not supported from it, because others preceded and acquired it, and maintenance and inheritance of the mother's ketubah are collected only from unencumbered property (see above, halachah 9, 18:13; for a similar law see Hilchot Zechiyah u-Matanah 8:9).

the daughter of a woman who refused. A minor who was married off after her father's death may refuse her husband and leave the marriage as long as she is a minor (see above 4:7-8). This one refused her husband after she became pregnant, and a daughter was born to her from him, and after his death the daughter claims maintenance.

and she has maintenance. Although the girl who refused herself loses the principal of her ketubah (below 24:5), she does not lose the conditions of the ketubah, and her daughter is entitled to maintenance (Yad Peshutah).

the daughter of a yevamah. Who was born from her mother's marriage to the yavam, the brother of her first husband who died. If her father the yavam dies, she has no maintenance from him, since the yevamah's ketubah and its conditions are imposed on the property of the brother who died, not on the yavam's property (below 22:11, Hilchot Yibbum va-Chalitzah 1:1).

and the daughter of a sheniyah. Whose mother was forbidden to her husband by rabbinic enactment (for the definition see above 1:6), and she has no ketubah and no conditions of the ketubah (below 24:2).
and the daughter of an arusah. Whose mother became pregnant by her father before they married, when the husband was not yet obligated for a ketubah.

and the daughter of an anusah. A girl who was raped and married her rapist and bore him a daughter. Since the husband may not divorce his raped wife, she has no ketubah, for the Sages enacted a ketubah for a woman so that it would not be light in his eyes to divorce her, and he cannot divorce her (Hilchot Na'arah Betulah 1:3-4).

like the law of other sons and daughters during their father's lifetime. For this obligation is not on account of the ketubah, but because of the father's duty to provide for his children (see above 12:14-15).

obligated for her maintenance from the time of betrothal. Although in general the husband is obligated for maintenance only from the time of marriage (for another case of maintenance from betrothal see above 10:19).

even if she is awaiting a yavam etc.. Her husband died without children, and although she is waiting for yibbum or chalitzah, she is not considered thereby bound to the husband with regard to maintenance.

for it is possible that the sons and daughters can be supported from them together until the daughters come of age. Based on an estimate of the maintenance needed for all of them together for this period.

they take out of them maintenance for the daughters. They set aside from the inheritance the entire amount needed for the daughters' food until they come of age, and leave it in the hands of the court or a guardian.
and the sons shall ask at the doors. They will beg for alms. For there is no condition of maintenance for sons, only inheritance.
and by the enactment of the Geonim. Above 16:7.
the daughters and sons are supported together from the property. And the daughters have no preference as in the previous halachah.
and they decreased. Their value fell.
the heirs have already acquired them. The sons. And they support their sisters as long as there is unencumbered property.

if the sons preceded and sold the small amount of property, their sale stands. The sale is valid. And the daughters cannot seize from the buyers, since they are supported only from unencumbered property (above 18:13).
or he stipulated with his wife that he would support her daughter. Born to her from another man. For this too is a type of debt (see below 23:17-18).
the widow is supported and the daughter asks at the doors. For his wife's honor comes before his daughter's honor (Bavli Ketubot 40a).

for the daughter's maintenance precedes the son's inheritance of his mother's ketubah who died during his father's lifetime. The daughter's maintenance allowance must be set aside, and only if money remains is the condition of the ketubah of male children fulfilled. If the Torah's inheritance is set aside because of the daughter's maintenance. For when the property is small, the daughters are supported and the sons inherit nothing, as above, halachah 17.

we do not say: let the minors be supported until they come of age etc.. For the condition of maintenance is a rabbinic enactment for daughters when the sons inherit all the property. But when there are no sons, by Torah law the daughters inherit all the property, and the Sages did not enact maintenance for them.
one who marries off his daughter plainly. Without saying what he gives his daughter for her marriage.
as we have explained. Above 13:1-5.
he specified it against the husband. The father explicitly agreed with the husband before the marriage.
she has nothing. The father is not obligated to clothe her.
when she comes to my house I will clothe her. I will clothe her only after I marry her.
and his acquaintances. His familiar associates.
if he married off a daughter in his lifetime, they estimate by her. They estimate on the basis of the amount he gave this daughter when he married her off.
they give her a tenth of his property for her support. A tenth of his property.
a tenth of what the first one left. A tenth of the property remaining after the first daughter took.
and if all of them came to marry at once. At the same time.
even if there are ten of them. For by this calculation property will remain for the brothers, and the inheritance, which is from the Torah, will not be nullified.
and they divide all the tenths equally. They divide equally among themselves the total of the tenths that all of them received.
it is not among the conditions of the ketubah. Which are listed above 12:2.
even according to the enactment of the later authorities. The Geonim, who enacted that the ketubah is collected even from movables (above 16:7).
and she may collect this tenth from the rental of the land. She may also take from the rent of the land to others, for this too is like collecting from land.
money in place of a tenth of the land. Money equal to the value of the land.
from the average. From land of medium quality, as with a creditor.
from the zibburit. Poor land.
and by oath. That she took nothing from the property.
in Hilchot Loans. Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 14:1, 19:1.
that they pledged. They gave the land as security for a loan.
the daughter seizes from the buyers. She has the right to take the land from the buyers.
in Hilchot Loans. Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 18:1.

they do not take support for the minors... but all divide equally. The gift of a tenth of the property for the daughters' support was enacted only where there is a son, in which case the daughters have no inheritance. But when there are no sons, the daughters inherit everything by Torah law.
we have already explained. Above 19:21.

she does not take a tenth of the property because of the widow's maintenance. For the widow is entitled to sell the father's property that the daughter inherited, for her maintenance, as long as there is need, even if the property is completely used up.

the husband does not inherit the support that should be given to her. And we do not say that the husband is considered to have bought the property and the widow's lien no longer applies to it (above 18:13), but he is considered an heir from whom property is taken for the widow's maintenance.
with her consent. With her agreement.
and even if the brothers were not supporting her. For if they were supporting her, she could claim that she did not protest because of that, as below in the next halachah.
and even though she did not protest. Although she did not protest and did not express her objection to not receiving the support proper to her, we do not conclude from this that she waived her right.
for a minor is not capable of protest. She has no understanding with which to protest.
if the daughter married... and did not claim her support, she lost her support. We must assume she waived her right.
and if she protested at the time of her marriage. And stated explicitly that she does not waive.
the brothers stopped her maintenance. They stopped supporting her.
as we have explained. Above 19:10.
and they supported her as an adult. While she was an adult. Although they are not obligated to.

because they support her though they are not obligated, and she has not yet married. She is embarrassed to claim her support from them because they support her voluntarily, and the time has not yet come to collect her support (as above, halachah 4).
to buy land with them. To purchase land for her.
one who is deathly ill. Dangerously ill and about to die.
whether he was healthy and died. For it is a mitzvah to fulfill his words (Hilchot Zechiyah u-Matanah 4:5).
and the money is in the hand of the agent. The money was deposited with another person, who is to carry out the father's mission.
the agent shall do what was entrusted to his hand. The agent shall do what the father determined, that is, buy land.
and what does she do for him. What tasks must the woman do for her husband.
to spin wool or flax. To twist threads from them.

for flax harms the mouth and the lips. For in spinning they moisten the threads with saliva, and flax causes bad breath and the fibers may wound the lips. 2. She pushed herself and did more than was fitting for her. She exerted herself greatly and produced more than she was supposed to do.
lewdness. Acts of immorality.
and one who binds his wife by a vow. Forbids her something by a vow.
and she mixes his cup. Prepares for him a cup of wine to drink.
in front of his son. The son of her husband.
she herself does them. For in these acts there is intimacy.
and Ezra. The scribe, at the beginning of the Second Temple period, who enacted many ordinances in matters of Torah (see for example Hilchot Tefillah 1:2) and conduct (see for example below 24:13).
and she gives straw in front of his animal. That he rides.
but not in front of his cattle. That serve for the household's livelihood.
and she hurries the grinder. She urges on the woman grinding.
she drives behind the animal. She leads the animal that turns the millstones.
and if it was their custom to grind with hand mills. If their custom is that the lady of the house grinds the flour they need herself, on household mills.
she brought in for him. She brought in her property at the time of marriage.
and she does not nurse her son. She is not obligated to nurse.
all the work that a woman does for her husband etc.. For a similar law see Hilchot Issurei Biah 11:19.
a woman who broke vessels... is exempt. From payment for the damage she caused.
they seat a woman among them or neighbors. To see whether the woman fulfills her duties.
they reduce her handiwork. They reduce the amount of work required of her.
for they are good for milk. They improve its quality.
she will become disfigured. She will become unsightly.
for a woman rises with her husband and does not descend. Regarding status (see also above 19:11, 14:23).
she must bring proof, and there is no room for an oath. Because she wants to be released from her obligation, and she can do so only with proof.
he gives her her wages. As a wet nurse. For the duty to support the children rests on the father (above 12:14).
even if he was blind. Because the infant is attached to his mother even if he does not see her.
and anointing. With oil.
the pregnant woman. His divorcee, who became pregnant before he divorced her.
his months were completed. Twenty-four months have passed (as above, halachah 13).
they do not separate him from her until he is a full six years old. They do not separate them, for up to this age the son is attached to his mother.
the father may. He is permitted.
I will give him nothing. For the father's duty to support his sons applies until age six (above 12:14).
how so. What is the obligation of support for a daughter who is with her mother.
if the father was fit for charity. A man of means who can give from his money to charity (see above 12:15).
by the condition of the ketubah. For one of the conditions is that the daughters be supported from his property after his death (above 12:2, 19:10).
if the mother does not wish etc.. For the duty to support the children rests on the father and not on her (above 12:14).
a husband precedes everyone in inheriting his wife. This is one of the conditions of the ketubah (above 12:3, Hilchot Nachalot 1:8).
that she enters the chuppah. That he brings her to his home and is alone with her (above 10:1).
even though her ketubah is still in her father's house. Although the property written in her ketubah, which her father granted her for her marriage, is still in her father's house.
with the husband. One who goes to be alone with his wife. 3. An adult, an orphan, or a widow. Who are not under their father's authority but under their own (above 3:12).

one who marries a woman who is forbidden to him. Forbidden by a prohibition of a negative or positive commandment, or because of the prohibition of sheniyot (see above 1:6-8), in which case the betrothal takes effect. But in the forbidden sexual relations the betrothal does not take effect (above 4:12-14), and he does not inherit her.
and likewise one who marries a minor. Who left her father's authority, for example because she was orphaned.
although her betrothal is not complete. For her betrothal is pending until she grows up (above 4:7-8).
if she dies under him he inherits her. For the Sages enacted for her a marriage similar to that of an adult.

but a hearing man who married a deaf woman, if she dies he does not inherit her. For the Sages did not enact a ketubah for a deaf woman so that men would not refrain from marrying her (above 11:4), and therefore he does not inherit her, since inheritance is part of the conditions of the ketubah (above 12:3; and see further Hilchot Nachalot 1:9).

and a deaf man who married a hearing woman inherits her, for she is of sound mind, married with her consent, and her property was acquired by him. Like any woman who married, for she is of sound mind and has in principle a right to a ketubah, although she does not actually receive it because of the deaf man's lack of understanding, since he cannot obligate himself in it (see above 11:6).
who was betrothed with her father's consent. With his will.
as we have explained. Above 3:13.
and even if the father was silent. And did not object, this is not consent (see there; and see further Hilchot Terumot 8:16).
for a woman who became ill etc.. She fears she will die, and wants her husband not to inherit her but her relatives.
they do not listen to her. They do not accept her claim.
and even if she said: I hate him etc.. For in an ordinary case, a woman who refuses to live with her husband is treated as a rebellious wife, and is divorced without her ketubah (above 14:8-14).
property of iron sheep and property of melog. Above 16:1.
the husband eats all their produce. He uses the profits that come from her property (and this is one of the conditions of the ketubah, above 12:3).
fell to her. She acquired them by inheritance.

the husband takes the produce out of the hands of the buyers. For his right in the produce overrides the buyers' right (see Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 26:12. On property of iron sheep see below, halachah 15).
if she died in his lifetime he takes the substance out of the buyers' hands without payment. Without payment. For his right in the land comes before the buyer's right.
and if the money she took from the buyers still exists in itself. The money the buyers paid is still in the woman's hands.
perhaps it is a find. Money that was found. And this is not the same money.

and the husband did not know of them... her sale stands. The husband did not take this property into account at the time of marriage, and therefore we cannot say that the woman was obligated not to sell it (Rashi Ketubot 78b).

a woman who wrote all her property to another, whether distant etc.. This woman wants her husband to have no rights in her property, and therefore wrote the property as a gift to another person, relative or distant. The law in this case is that if she is widowed or divorced, the property returns to her ownership.
as will be explained in Hilchot Gifts. Hilchot Zechiyah u-Matanah 6:12.

and she wrote to the recipient: acquire from today and whenever I wish. So that whenever she says she does not want the gift, she gets the property back. This wording is effective to cancel the sale even if she gave only part of the property.
a woman awaiting a yavam. A woman whose husband died without children, and who is waiting for his brother to marry her.
she may. She is permitted.
and the yavam has no produce. For in this situation he has no rights yet in her property.
until he enters. Until he performs yibbum with his brother's wife.
her heirs from her father inherit her melog property. For this property was in her possession even while she was married, and only the produce belongs to the husband (see above 16:1).

and half the property of iron sheep. This property was in the husband's possession (there), and had she entered yibbum it would have passed to the yavam, and had she performed chalitzah it would have been hers. Since her status was not decided, it is split between his heirs and hers.
and the husband's heirs inherit her ketubah. For it is a debt of the husband, and is in his possession.
and the husband's heirs are obligated for her burial. For the burial obligation corresponds to inheriting the ketubah (above 12:4; compare Hilchot Nachalot 3:9).

her ketubah is on all the property of her husband. All the property of her deceased husband is encumbered for payment of her ketubah, and the yavam does not write her a ketubah (see Hilchot Yibbum va-Chalitzah 1:1).
their produce. The profits that will come from that land.
and to forbid them to him by this guarantee. To forbid him to sell this property because it is encumbered for payment of the ketubah.
who had no ketubah. Her husband did not write her a ketubah, or she sold him her ketubah (Hilchot Yibbum va-Chalitzah 2:17).
a ketubah of a hundred. Like a widow (above 10:9).

she did nothing. The sale or gift to the husband does not take effect, because she did so for the sake of domestic peace (see below, halachot 17-18), and to others it does not take effect because of the husband's rights in the property (and see Hilchot Mechirah 30:3).
a husband who sold land etc.. For the woman has a right in the substance of the land, even in property of iron sheep.
for he is not permitted. Because of her right in that property.
his sale stands. For in movables her right is less than in land, since they may be used up and he will return their value (Maggid Mishneh, Hilchot Mechirah 30:5).
a field he designated for her in her ketubah. From which the ketubah is to be collected.
a field he wrote for her in her ketubah. To be as an addition to the ketubah.
or a field he brought in for her at a valuation from his own. That he gave her a specific field to add to the nedunya, in addition to the property she brought from her father's house (below 23:11).
that they made a kinyan from the woman. They performed an act of acquisition giving force to the undertaking.
the husband has no proof. Even if he proves that he bought the field from his wife.
as we have explained. In the previous halachah.
and she waived them. She forgave him his debt.

what is this like? Like one from whose hand they made a kinyan, who has no guarantee etc.. This case is like one in which the woman waived the husband's responsibility to preserve the value of the property, and changed its status to melog property, for which he has no responsibility. Such a waiver is effective if a kinyan of obligation was made on it, and the claim "I did a favor for my husband" does not apply here, since the husband receives nothing.
a husband who sold land for produce. He sold to another the right to eat the produce of melog property, while the substance of the land remained the woman's.
for they enacted produce for the man only in order to profit in the household expenses. So there would be additional income for supporting the household.
to do business with them. Which also allows profit for the household.
he may trade and transact with them. The husband is permitted to trade with them, and he will be obligated to return their value in the end.
these are sold and land is bought with all of it. So that the substance of the property is in the woman's hands and does not get used up.
all the money that should be given to her etc.. The money from the payments due to the woman in such a case. But the payments due to the husband are given to him immediately.
as will be explained in Hilchot Wounding. Hilchot Chovel u-Mazik 4:15.
they are not sold because of the honor of her father's house. For it is a slight to her family's honor that their property be in the hands of others.
and she had no part in the substance of the land in which the trees are. Only the fruit trees belong to her, not the area of the field.
they yield only the cost of their upkeep. Their income covers the cost of tending them.
they are sold for wood. For use in work or for fuel.
attached to the land, these belong to the husband. Since the land remains in her hands as melog property, the husband may eat its produce.
detached from her land etc.. For if he eats them, no principal remains for the woman.
but one who divorces his wife etc.. His right in her produce ends at the time of the divorce. If they were detached before the divorce, he acquired the produce.

the husband is obligated for their maintenance etc.. For with his own slaves he may say "work with me and I will not support you," and the slave will be supported from charity. But with melog slaves he took upon himself in advance the duty to support them, otherwise they would run away and the principal would be lost (Hilchot Avadim 9:7).
and they work for him and he eats their produce. They work for him, and he profits from their labor.
